#4746. I’ll Be 72 When My Youngest Kid Graduates High School. I Wouldn’t Have it Any Other Way.

“I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can,” says comedian Andy Richter.

I DON’T CONSIDER myself to be very “Hollywood,” but in terms of fatherhood, I’m practically a cliché.

It’s because I had my kids in waves. There’s my son Will, 26, and daughter Mercy, 21, from my first marriage, and my daughter Cornelia, 6, from my second and present marriage.

There are a lot of us old-dads-of-young-kids out here, and the main reason is that there are so many Los Angeles men who, after they get that first marriage out of the way, employ a sort of Benjamin Button philosophy towards the subsequent ones in that as time marches forward and the end of life moves closer, the wives get younger and younger.

I don’t lump myself in with those geezers, though, because I am 60 and my wife is 50, and the narrowness of that merely ten-year gap affords me the moral superiority of a guy married to someone with whom he can have actual conversations.

But the fact remains that I was 54 when my youngest was born. And yes, I have done all the math. I’ll be 72 when she graduates high school, 76 when she graduates college, and god knows what kind of drooling diapered mess I’ll be when I’m giving the toast at her wedding, champagne flute in one hand, the other one white-knuckling my walker.

But it is what it is. I fell in love with a single mother who, after many years of a successful career, wanted a child and hadn’t found a suitable partner to raise one with. A relationship with Jen was always going to be a package deal, and it’s the best one I’ve ever been lucky enough to gladly tumble head over heels into.

When I started letting people know that we were engaged and that I was going to adopt the then-two-year-old Cornelia (I was calling it “getting back into the toddler business”), people had one of two reactions.

The first was along the lines of Why the fuck would you do that? For so many people, and especially parents, the idea of going back to raising a pre-pre-schooler was incomprehensible. To them it was like driving through a hurricane and then making a U-ey to take one more crack at it for fun.

The other reaction was that I was some kind of saint. That to so selflessly dive back into the stress of making a person out of what is basically a little wild animal that can delete seven phone apps in less than one minute made me some sort of super dad, the menschiest of mensches.

This take was, while flattering, a little embarrassing, because years ago I figured out that all you have to do be hoisted on metaphorical shoulders and pronounced a Good Dad is about 30 percent of the work that it takes to be a Good Mom.

I also felt a little sheepish about the idea that signing up to help raise a two year old was somehow heroic because I knew that this little girl was giving me a gift: approximately 16 years of not having to figure out was I was going to do with myself.

“What should I do now?” has been a question that has plagued me for my entire life in both the micro and the macro. It’s why I smoked for almost 20 years. When you’re raising a child, you don’t have to come up with something to do—you’ve got that kid to take care of. You want a purpose? How about making a decent human?

When you are raising a child, it’s always good work. You are never wasting your time on an unworthy project. (A quick stroll through my IMDB page will show that I have done that more than a few times.)

So when a group of kindergarten girls asks me, “Are you Cornelia’s grandpa?” I just let it roll off my back, because they don’t know about the scam I’m running. I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can.

And there’s a good chance that by the time she’s ready to head out on her own, her older brother and sister might start having children, which means I will possibly get to have a life filled with babies and little kids for a long, long time. And that is a huge win for me.

I once heard Bob Odenkirk say on a podcast, “When you’re raising little kids, you know what your job is.” I know exactly what he means, and I love my job.

Andy Richter, author of Elf Unwrapped, is a Los Angeles–based comedian, actor, writer, and host best known as Conan O’Brien’s longtime sidekick, who also hosts the Three Questions podcast and The Andy Richter Call-In Show and had a longer-than-expected run on Dancing with the Stars.

#4745. Tesla hikes Cybertruck prices up to 10% after announcing it will kill production

Tesla has raised Cybertruck prices in the US by up to 10% and stopped taking orders for the base Dual Motor AWD trim. The cheapest Cybertruck you can actually order now costs $92,490.

The move comes right after Tesla confirmed it will end Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas around mid-2027.

Here’s what Tesla’s online configurator shows today, compared to the prices set in August:

The Dual Motor trim still shows a new, higher price on Tesla’s website, but the option is greyed out. So Tesla raised the price of a version it isn’t selling anymore.

This is the second price hike in less than three months. Tesla raised prices by $5,000 on two trims in August, when the Dual Motor went from $69,990 to $74,990 and the Premium AWD from $79,990 to $84,990.

Add it up and the Premium AWD is now $12,500 (15.6%) more expensive than it was in early August. And the entry price for any Cybertruck you can order went from $69,990 to $92,490. That’s a 32% jump in about 10 weeks.

For reference, Tesla unveiled the Cybertruck in 2019 with a promised starting price of $39,900.

The price hikes make little sense from a demand standpoint. Tesla doesn’t break out Cybertruck deliveries, but its “Other Models” category, which also includes the Model S, Model X, and Semi, fell 48% year-over-year to 8,295 units in Q3. We estimate Cybertrucks made up 7,000 to 8,000 of those, about 12% of the line’s 250,000-unit annual capacity.

Tesla also tried the opposite approach earlier this year. It offered a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 in February for “only the next 10 days,” then pulled it. A single-motor RWD version was discontinued after just 173 sales. None of it moved the needle.

The Cybertruck isn’t sold in Europe or most right-hand-drive markets, and Tesla canceled it for Australia and New Zealand last month.

So, Tesla has now discontinued more models than it currently offers. Looks like the great leader isn’t particularly good at writing product specs. And the hype has been over for quite a while anyway. In Europe, owning a Tesla has actually become something of an image liability.

This is what a wind-down looks like. Tesla isn’t trying to sell more Cybertrucks anymore. It’s trying to make as much money as possible on the last ones, with the hope that announcing the end of production will encourage some people to secure their order.

Once you’ve decided to end a program, volume stops mattering. You have a set number of build slots left, a parts supply you want to burn down, and probably a small group of fans who’ll want one before it’s gone. Pausing the cheapest trim and charging $7,500 more for the rest is the obvious play. You push everyone into higher-margin configurations and stop pretending the base truck is a real product.

But it does say a lot about the last two years of Cybertruck pricing. Tesla went from a $59,990 “limited-time” offer in February to a $92,490 entry price in November. That’s a company that never figured out who the truck was for.

#4744. 5 New Retail Design Rules, According to Experts

When nearly anything can be bought with a few taps on a screen, brick-and-mortar stores have to work harder—and smarter—to earn a visit. What e-commerce can't replicate, even with the cleverest algorithms, is the thrill of stepping into a beautifully conceived space—and discovering something you didn't know you wanted. From side-by-side jewel-box fashion boutiques in Paris to a palatial bridal studio set in a 19th-century building in downtown New York, AD PRO highlights the big ideas shaping today’s most engaging retail environments.

The first goal for any new retail space is obvious: Make people want to be there.

Fashion designer Danielle Frankel Hirsch just opened a 12,000-square-foot studio in Tribeca, collaborating with Studio Partners Architecture and AD PRO Directory designer Augusta Hoffman to create a gasp-worthy dress boutique worthy of any bride's fantasies. Located in a 19th century edifice originally built to house the New York Mercantile Exchange, the shop, says Frankel Hirsch, is designed as a transportive experience. After guests enter the space through its unassuming Tribeca storefront entrance, they ascend a grand carpeted staircase to a large gallery boasting over 30-foot floor-to-ceiling windows. Hoffman worked with artist Miriam Ellner to create églomisé paneling surrounding the staircase, and outfitted the spaces to the height of elegance, with Fortuny fabrics, furniture sourced from Paris, and handpainted ceiling murals.

The 30-foot ceilings at New York City's Danielle Frankel guarantee a wedding dress shopping experience that's hard to equal

In Paris, Rubirosa's two petite boutiques, designed by Louis Charles Aka, deliver a similar sense of occasion on a much smaller scale. The original 500-square-foot shop, which opened in June 2025, was joined this past August by a second location just next door. Rather than simply duplicate the first boutique's nostalgic formality, Aka has given its new neighbor a distinct personality. The lacquered shelving remains, displaying cashmere sweaters, crisp poplin shirts, and soft leather slippers in a rainbow of colors. But where the original featured tall bookcases, the new shop has floor-to-ceiling arches whose cubbies become bands of color when filled with garments of cashmere, cotton, and silk.

In the original boutique, the defining gesture was a dense, velvety red wall-to-wall carpet from La Maison Bineau. “I spent everything on the red carpet,” Aka declares. “People criticized, ‘You will have to change it in three months.’ I said, ‘We don’t care. We want people to feel special.’” In the second shop, the color drama comes courtesy of vivid Yves Klein blue—a knowing wink to the fashion set. Voluminous white balloon drapery heightens the theatricality, suggesting a salon for elegant grand dames even as the boutique attracts a younger crowd of influencers and trendsetters.

Lacquered walls hung with portraits of Pope John Paul II and Mobutu Sese Seko at Rubirosa’s

The exterior of Rubirosa’s on Rue de Grenelle in Paris

AD100 designer Brigette Romanek took a more subtle approach to creating desire at Catherine Bloom for Nordstrom, an appointment-only shop in Los Angeles where Bloom, the department store’s Director of Luxury Styling, works with private clients. “I want to make people feel something,” says Romanek. “A store should be a destination you look forward to.” Her use of paneled walls in camel, khaki, and rose suede, plus her signature mix of elements both edgy (the angular leather sofa) and delicate (the plasterwork ceiling) creates what she calls “a protected feeling” that makes the space feel worth seeking out.

Suede-paneled walls and ornate plasterwork at Catherine Bloom for Nordstrom

A punchy red-orange “wallop” moment at Big Night’s West Village outpost

Where Romanek’s space whispers intimacy, Katherine Lewin’s Big Night shouts joy. The New York City shop Big Night, which sells brightly hued kitchen and entertaining goods, trades old-world refinement for modern exuberance. “People tell me they get a shot of serotonin walking into the store,” she says. Her brand’s signature color of punchy red-orange provides what she calls a “wallop”—an immediate sensory experience that registers before customers even process what they’re looking at. Handmade tiles from Smink Studio, screen-printed with bold geometric patterns, are mixed in unexpected color combinations throughout the West Village store.

FoundRae’s Aspen boutique, complete with velvety chairs, books, and intriguing display cases lined with handwritten letters, old photos, and found objects

Once you’ve lured customers in, the next challenge is keeping them there. “If someone is waiting for their partner to try on 50 things, they need to be comfortable,” says Romanek, who installed upholstered chairs from her collection for Crate & Barrel inside individual dressing rooms. Meanwhile, curtains at the store stay closed at all times, enhancing the protected atmosphere that encourages clients to relax and take their time.

Beth Hutchens, founder of fine jewelry line FoundRae, has turned lingering into an art form. The average customer stay at her fine jewelry boutiques—which include locations in New York, Miami, Los Angeles, Dallas, Palm Beach, and Aspen—is an hour and a half. It makes sense when you consider the cozy reading nooks well stocked with books and a rotating menu of complimentary snacks and wine.

The maze-like layout of Big Night’s West Village

In the age of algorithmic shopping recommendations, physical retail can offer something genuinely different: the pleasure of stumbling upon the unexpected. When Lewin found Big Night’s West Village location, for instance, it was a warren of small spaces and hidden corners that defied traditional notions of retail design. Rather than optimizing for efficient shopping (and increasing her renovation costs), she embraced the pre-existing layout and discovered that it primed shoppers’ sense of exploration and surprise. “The store feels like a house party with different things happening in different corners,” Lewin explains.

At Fishs Eddy's Brooklyn location, deliberately cluttered displays add to the sense of discovery

At Fishs Eddy, the beloved New York City housewares shop founded in 1986, the thrill of the hunt has always been part of the appeal. Now, four decades after opening its original Manhattan location, the retailer has expanded with two new outposts, at Chelsea Market and in Brooklyn's Dumbo neighborhood. The latter, an ambitious 3,800-square-foot space, deliberately preserves the cheerfully cluttered, homespun aesthetic that has become the brand's calling card. Rather than give the larger store a slick makeover, founder Julie Gaines embraced the same informal, decidedly human approach to retail design: Vintage-style dishes, deadstock dinnerware, and offbeat glassware are piled high on reclaimed-wood displays and mismatched vintage furniture, evoking the warehouses where the original merchandise was discovered. Gaines describes her merchandising philosophy as “very direct: the way we found it in the warehouse.” But that seemingly improvised look takes effort. “We spend a lot of time looking like we don’t spend time,” she admits. An old-fashioned soda fountain serving egg creams and inexpensive drip coffee adds to the new store's convivial atmosphere.

FoundRae takes discovery to remarkable lengths. Hutchens installed fully realized miniature vignettes behind unmarked cupboard doors—doll-size rooms that include recreations of her own home and FoundRae boutiques, complete with furniture and art. Display cases feature what Hutchens calls a “menagerie of the ephemeral”—handwritten letters, old photos, and evocative found items loosely pinned behind the jewelry. Then there are the “Discovery Drawers”—wood-fronted, glass-topped compartments that hold one-of-a-kind pieces unique to each location (never photographed or featured online).

At Sézane’s new 2,800-square-foot boutique on New York’s Upper East Side, designer Pierre Lacroix has created a similar element of surprise through a dramatic shift in mood. Dubbed L’Appartement on Madison Avenue, the space evokes a Parisian home crossed with an art gallery, with books, artwork by William Klein, and vintage furniture. Most of the boutique feels light and airy, with creamy walls, cerused oak parquet floors, and parchment light fixtures. But tucked off to one side is a small shoe salon, drenched in dark chocolate tones and moodily lit. The intimate, after hours lounge-like space offers an unexpected counterpoint to the rest of the shop.

Sézane’s newest shop, aka L’Appartement on Madison Avenue, designed by Pierre Lacroix

The shoe salon at Sézane’s L’Appartement offers an unexpected change of atmosphere

Even in Rubirosa’s tiny space, Aka has created moments of discovery. He’s filled the walls with oil portraits of Luciano Pavarotti, Pope John Paul II, and various international dictators—a quirky mix of imagery that gives the space a distinctive personality. Visual layers invite clients to continuously notice new details, rewarding repeat visits.

Wes Anderson calling! A particularly Instagrammable corner of Rubirosa’s

Aka admits that Rubirosa’s Instagram-friendly storefront serves as what he calls “a lure”—beautiful enough that people stop to photograph it even if they don’t come inside. “Some people come just to take pictures in front,” he says. The combination of the crimson carpet, dark lacquered millwork, and those quirky framed portraits creates an irresistibly photogenic and TikTok-friendly environment. Romanek’s thoughtful color palette and material mix at the Nordstrom boutique creates a similarly camera-ready backdrop. The social media effect, says Romanek, is simply a natural byproduct of creating a distinctive space. “When a space feels different, conversations about it happen,” she explains. “And that’s what we like. We like people talking about the experience.”

At the Danielle Frankel bridal studio, the sheer spectacle reaches another level entirely. From the soaring ceilings to the grand staircase with its shimmering églomisé panels, the interiors offer no shortage of photo opportunities. But for a boutique devoted to dressing brides for what is, ideally, a once-in-a-lifetime occasion, perhaps a little over-the-top grandeur is exactly the point.

Hoffman worked with the artist Miriam Ellner to create églomisé paneling surrounding the staircase. “The eglomise is one of my favorite things,” says Danielle Frankel designer Frankel Hirsch. The result is staircase that not creates a heightened emotional atmosphere for in-store shoppers but also provides a dramatic backdrop for photography.

Hutchens believes retail design isn’t inextricably tied to scalability. “Ask yourself, if every store was your only store, what would you do and how would you invest in it and change it?” she says. “You evolve faster when you think that way.”

While all seven FoundRae stores share some design DNA—Hutchens embeds her signature mythological symbols in floors, ceilings, and furniture throughout—each reflects its location. The Aspen boutique is swathed in green, alluding to the town’s namesake aspen trees, with a large marquetry sunburst as its centerpiece. The Palm Beach shop features gilded verre églomisé, while in Miami, a vintage Steinway grand piano with hand-applied gold symbols anchors the room. As a result, the stores feel both part of a cohesive brand while rooted in their specific communities.

Big Night’s location in Brooklyn’s Greenpoint

Even Lewin’s three Big Night locations—Brooklyn, West Village, and the Upper East Side, which she calls “sisters, not twins”—each have distinct personalities while maintaining the brand’s joyful, color-saturated identity. Lewin likens the Upper East Side shop to a Classic Six apartment and notes that the new millwork was designed to reflect an upscale, elevated home. Her cash desk placement in the West Village location, situated in the center of the largest room rather than tucked away, came from understanding that specific space and how her team could best interact with customers there.

The thread connecting these diverse approaches is a fundamental understanding that physical retail can no longer compete with e-commerce on convenience or selection. But the best retail spaces offer atmosphere, discovery, community, and the experience of being somewhere that feels genuinely special. As Aka puts it, “Like a good movie, when it ends...if you don’t have the feeling you want to see it again, it was not that good.”

The back room of Rubirosa’s is painted in a pale baby blue, “like a boy’s little bedroom,” says Aka. “So when you take out your credit card, it doesn’t bother you. It’s like you’re on a pillow.”

A leather, steel, and palmwood sofa by Pacific Green at Catherine Bloom for Nordstrom, designed by AD100 talent Brigette Romanek

The only caveat is Flawless is a razor, so it cuts hair at the top layer of skin, meaning hair will grow back relatively fast. So, as long as you don't mind regular trims, this is an epic choice.

After two years of on-and-off testing, Flamingo still makes my favorite razor. Its sharp blades that don’t tug or pull at my sensitive skin elevate Flamingo to the top of my shower routine.

Plus, this razor set is comfy to use while shaving down to my ankles. It curves along my kneecaps and pits with ease, and it hasn’t caused any nicks or ingrown hairs along my bikini line.

I’ll continue using Flamingo, and at just $16, you can also enjoy smooth skin which includes the razor, four blades, and a holder that fits neatly in cramped spaces like my New York City shower.

While I don't mind using a traditional manual razor or dermaplaning, it's worth spending a little extra on this electric device, says Wohlner. Wohlner's been using this facial hair removal tool for hairs and considers it the most effective method for eliminating stubborn upper lip and chin hairs. Pro tip: The large shaver head does tend to get clogged after a few uses, which can be prevented if you wipe it down with alcohol after every use. Taking care of your device will ensure you get the closest shave and that it lasts for years.

The idea of gliding a sharp razor across my face was initially intimidating, but I haven't scratched myself since using the Dermaflash. This hair removal cream isn't the Nair you grew up on. It's a prescription-strength cream specifically formulated to slow hair growth on the face. Each batch is compounded together shortly before shipping, ensuring maximum potency.

I've tried many hair removal creams, which sometimes cause redness and irritation, so I was worried Musely would be a problem. It has a light tingling sensation, letting me know the cream is working. Unlike cheaper drugstore alternatives, Musely hasn't irritated my skin. It also doesn't have a super aggressive chemical smell like other alternatives I tested, and that alone is a win in my book.

The major downside of hair removal creams, including Musely, is that I have to adjust when I use my tretinoin prescription around hair removal days. After Musely hair removal, I typically wait a few days before safely applying my tretinoin cream. Otherwise, I might experience redness, irritation, and over-exfoliate my skin. Musely is a worthwhile product, but I prefer dermaplaning or shaving because I value acne-free skin over a fast-acting, pain-free hair removal process.

Your hair color, skin color, and hair thickness helps determine your best facial hair removal method, says dermatologist Blair Murphy-Rose, MD. They are epic when you have dark hair and a fair to medium complexion; particularly those with thick, coarse and unruly dark chin, upper lip, and sideburn hair. But if you're a four or deeper on the Fitzpatrick Scale like me, you should skip using at-home laser hair removal devices. "You want to receive the right treatment that does not harm your skin," dermatologist Jeanine Downie, MD, previously told WH.

They work by slowing hair growth and reducing strand thickness by using highly concentrated light to penetrate hair follicles and inhibit future hair growth. While laser hair removal isn't exactly permanent, it can effectively slow hair growth. This is my go-to hair removal method because of the low upkeep. I can easily go 4-6 weeks between my sessions, but TBH, I'll stretch it to every 8 weeks. I've been waxing for years and find the pain has become quite tolerable. On a scale of 1 to 10, waxing my face and underarms ranges from 2—3 and 4—6 elsewhere on my body, with the most painful spots being the back of my legs and bikini area. Sugaring It is similar to waxing but less painful. I've had some uncomfy waxes that stung my sensitive skin, but sugaring is noticeably milder. Ingredients will vary among brands, but there is almost always a mix of sugar, water, and lemon. The golden paste is molded onto your skin where you'd like to remove hair, and you'll gently remove it with a fast flicking technique like waxing.

These are tried-and-true hair removal tools that are cheap, readily accessible, and provide instant results. Your best bet is to use a razor with a non-slip ergonomic handle to keep your shave steady. I also like razors featuring a lubricating strip to help prevent irritation. Depending on how fast your facial hair regrows, you might need to shave daily or every few days, but they're pain-free. Remember to use shaving cream and gently run the blade in the opposite direction of hair growth. There are also manual and electric razors, but I'll discuss that more in the next section.

They feature surgical blades to remove dead skin cells and peach fuzz from your face. These devices also have long handles and sturdy grips to prevent accidental cuts. Because dermaplaning sloughs off dead skin cells, this hair removal tool provides the smoothest makeup application.

This method helps promote cell turnover and collagen production plus minimizes dark spots and uneven skin texture, dermatologist Azadeh Shirazi, MD, told WH. "When your skin is hairless and buildup-free, it looks super toned and bright," Dr. Shirazi said.

Since dermaplaning cuts the hairs at the top layer of skin, they'll grow back quicker than laser hair removal or waxing, says Dr. Murphy-Rose. So be ready to use this technique 1-4 times monthly, depending on how fast your hair regrows.

These creams typically contain ingredients like eflornithine, calcium hydroxide, calcium thioglycolate, sodium hydroxide, and sodium thioglycolate to dissolve keratin bond structures of strands, making them pain-free alternatives to tweezing, waxing, and sugaring. Let the cream sit for a few minutes, then wipe it away to reveal smoother skin. If your skin is super sensitive, you could leave it on for 1-3 minutes and then shave it off in warm water, dermatologist S. Manjula Jegasothy, MD, previously told us. Hair will begin to grow back within a few days, so you're looking at a low-key commitment.

These are best for removing hair from a small area of the face, like your eyebrows, chin, and upper lip. TBH, tweezing has mild to moderate discomfort since you're plucking hairs from the root. On a scale of 1—10, I'd rank the pain level from 4—6. Since I have sensitive eyes that easily water, I stay away from tweezing my brows, but I found plucking a rogue chin hair pretty mild. Upkeep depends on how fast your hair grows back. Some women want to pluck every few days, while others can stretch their tweezing schedule to every few weeks.

Dermaplaning tools and razors are either manual or electric powered by batteries or a USB or USB-C cable.

When you pick electric devices like the Dermaflash, you'll be spending around $200, while manual tools, including hair removal creams and razors are much cheaper. With prices ranging from $150 to $600, epilators and laser hair removal devices are definite investments, but still cost less than a series of professional sessions. Some of these splurge-worthy devices also have smart capabilities like Bluetooth, smartphone app features, and even calendar reminders to remove facial hair.

Ultimately, opt for the electric devices if you want a fast and powerful tool that lasts for years and don't mind the upfront cost. Choose a manual tool if you would rather save the cash for other beauty products, like an LED face mask or a red light therapy device for hair growth.

Keeping the above guidelines in mind—type, cost, and manual versus electric devices—I carefully researched dozens of at-home facial hair removal tools. After settling on 12 contenders, I spent several months testing and I was only truly impressed by a handful of picks. I evaluated their ease of use, how often I needed to remove hair, and how seamless they were to incorporate into my routine. Many at-home devices can’t distinguish between darker complexions and dark hair, dermatologist Dr. Nazarian previously told WH. Melanin-rich skin is at a higher risk of their skin absorbing laser hair and burning, said Dr. Nazarian. My advice: Either opt for a different alternative on this list or book an appointment with your dermatologist for specific guidance on the best laser hair removal treatment plan for you.

#4742. Pope Leo XIV Diagnosed With Lung Cancer After Surgery to Remove Part of Lung

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer following a successful surgery, the Vatican said.

The Pope, 71, underwent surgery at Agostino Gemelli University Policlinic in Rome on October 13 to remove a nodule from his right lung. This was determined to be pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

The surgeons removed the lower lobe of the Pope’s lung to “ensure a radical procedure; the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the Director of Vatican Healthcare Services, and Professor Stephano Margaritora, the lead surgeon, in a press release.

“An intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the preoperative examinations,” they said.

Pope Leo was in the operating room for 3 hours, while the operation itself lasted around 90 minutes.

The doctors noted that it was a successful operation with no complications.

According to Matteo Bruni, the Director of the Holy See Press Office, the Pope asked for dinner after the surgery and spent the evening with his secretaries and other Vatican staff.

In a press release on Wednesday, the Vatican said that the Pope’s postoperative recovery is progressing well.

According to Vatican News, Pope Leo had a calm first night following his surgery.

In the coming days, exams will be conducted on the removed tissue. There has currently been no change in the initially announced week of hospitalization.

On October 14, the Pope underwent blood tests and chest X-rays that were scheduled following his surgery. The results of these tests confirm that his postoperative recovery is progressing as expected, and the values are within a normal range for the type of operation performed.

Pope Leo has also undergone some respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room, the Vatican said.

It has not yet been announced whether he will require any further treatment.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer globally. It accounts for around 40% of all lung cancer diagnoses.

Adenocarcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which accounts for about 80–85% of all lung cancers.

Lung adenocarcinoma begins in the epithelial cells that produce mucus. It is the most common type of NSCLC.

Adenocarcinoma can be classified further by the genetic changes driving the tumor. For example, EGFR-positive lung cancer is found more often in people who have never smoked and can often be treated with targeted therapies, which is why biomarker testing of tumor tissue helps guide treatment decisions.

Treatment for NSCLC is generally determined by the stage. However, it typically involves one or a combination of:

Surgery is generally the first step in treatment for this type of lung cancer. The right lung has three lobes, or sections, and the left has two.

A doctor will often remove the entire lobe that has the tumor in order to remove the tumor and improve the outlook.

The body eventually adapts in order to compensate for the loss of function.

According to the American Cancer Society (ACS), for NSCLC that hasn’t spread outside of the lung, the 5-year relative survival rate is 67%.

#4739. The Customer Loyalty Secret? It’s Not Just About Shopping

Imagine you’re at home one morning—settled in, slippers on, cozy. Your kids are playing in the next room. A couple of miles away, your local Pottery Barn is hosting a bed-styling workshop: You’ll learn how to layer coverlets and quilts, mix patterns, and plan for seasonality. And maybe at the end of it, you’ll get a small discount for an in-store purchase.

Do you go? Or, do you hop onto YouTube or TikTok and search for “bed-styling ideas”—slippers still on? Maybe you find what you’re looking for on Pottery Barn’s own YouTube channel. Maybe you search for some quilts like those you saw in the video, and—what’s this? A similar-looking option for less, from another brand that isn’t Pottery Barn?

Getting people out of their slippers and into the store—again and again—is one challenge that pros like Evan Hutton, McGee & Co.’s head of retail store operations and a veteran of the industry, are taking seriously. “It used to be you could just do a bed-styling class or [a class on] how to decorate a mantel, and people would come for that,” she says. No longer: Thanks to YouTube tutorials, the lure has to be much more compelling. The promise of social and experiential elements like gelato carts or floral-arranging workshops give customers a social and sensory reason to show up, she says. This strategy for cultivating customer loyalty is already making its way into the first McGee & Co. flagship in Salt Lake City, which opened in September.

Retails are seeing a growing interest for hands-on events, like this keychain-making activity at McGee & Co.

Shea McGee's finished keychain, complete with a monogram.

“I think of in-store programming as retail theater,” says Geri Moran, vice president of marketing at ABC Carpet & Home, a longtime New York City home shopping mecca. The beauty of programming, she notes, is that it brings together “commerce, culture, and discovery.” Importantly, it doesn’t even need to produce a sale right away, either. “It can build awareness, strengthen relationships with the design community, introduce new customers to the store, and give existing customers another reason to return,” she says.

During the holiday season, ABC Carpet & Home hosts carolers at its NYC flagship as a way to “give [customers] a reason to visit, connect, and come back,” says Moran.

She points to a caroling event held at ABC during the holiday season. Those fa-la-las aren’t frivolous: They’re how ABC makes an emotional imprint on its community, even if it may have very little to do with a specific product. “The merchandise gives people a reason to shop,” she says, “but the experience gives them a reason to visit, connect, and come back.”

Another way to get people coming back? Introduce elements that can only be discovered in person, whether that’s through store design, specialty goods, or locally made wares. Across the industry, brands are tackling this in a few different ways. McGee & Co., for one, is planning to include regional variations on their signature design language across its outposts as they expand across the US. Syd McGee, the company’s CEO, imagines a McGee fan encountering the store in different cities, each location informed by local culture. How does McGee do Texas versus California? There’s only one way to find out, he says.

The business is also embracing the potential of merchandise that can only be purchased in-store. At the opening of their Salt Lake City flagship, McGee & Co. offered gardening gear, Cire Trudon candles, Match pewter, and vintage pieces only shoppable in person. Though customers may have initially come to the flagship to check out a new piece of furniture, they’ll discover that their local store can also be a resource for gifts and one-off finds from the McGee universe.

The Lawson-Fenning showroom creates a welcoming environment for clients.

Lawson-Fenning, a homeware brand that has built a reputation for California-inflected design, takes a similar approach to layering, blending their own collection with vintage they’ve found and work from makers they admire. “There’s always something they didn’t come in for,” says cofounder Grant Fenning, adding that “plenty of our longtime clients first walked in without a plan.” While much of their consumer base encounters the brand for the first time through a designer, shoppers will often return on their own a year or two later.

A retailer’s job isn’t just to showcase hero products—it’s to build a world. Which might be why Il Buco Vita, a lifestyle brand offshoot of Il Buco’s hospitality business, does around 60 percent of its business in person, despite having a website full of products. Founder Donna Lennard notes that art, antiques, and decorative pieces frequently sell more in store, while online sales skew toward more everyday kitchen and dining products. “It all comes down to keeping the discovery process interesting,” says Lennard. “With each person that walks through the door, there is an opportunity to introduce them to something they might not have known they were looking for,” she says.

The associates working the showroom floor help complete the picture, educating customers about the artisans, product pairings, and long-term care of pieces. But this year, Il Buco Vita is taking their world-building efforts one step further by opening a new retail flagship on Bond Street, just a few doors down from their original restaurant. This proximity, Lennard says, “creates a stronger connection between hospitality and home,” and provides a setting to present larger pieces, antiques, and collections in a more experiential atmosphere. “Customers can see how they live together and imagine them in their own homes.”

Every issue, every era. Explore 100+ years of the Architectural Digest Archive, an unparalleled digital resource for research and inspiration. Start Searching

Across the board, the brands interviewed for this story identified trust as the key ingredient in creating repeat customers. Cultivating it begins from the moment someone begins engaging with your team—and it doesn’t end when the credit card swipes. “The sale isn’t truly complete when the customer pays,” Moran says. “It’s complete when the product has arrived, the customer is happy with it, and the experience makes them want to return.”

Associates’ product knowledge is the first half of the equation. Customers depend on sales staff to understand not just a product, but the whole-room experience that brands can deliver. This expertise also supports conversations on pricing. In the showroom, customers can test-drive a sofa, run their fingers across different types of upholstery, and scrutinize construction alongside an associate, who can help them unpack the differences between two similar models. “The conversation then becomes less about price and more about value, craftsmanship, longevity, and whether the product is right for the customer,” says Moran. “Our team can also help identify alternatives when something isn’t the right fit for a customer’s budget.”

Hutton notes that for McGee & Co., there was a deliberate decision made to refer to in-store employees as “design associates.” “When a customer comes in, we don’t want it to be, ‘Oh, let me take you over to the design concierge,’” says Hutton. “We want all our team members to be able to start those conversations—and oftentimes finish them too.”

Shea McGee, who briefed many of those first-time flagship associates herself, notes that education on the product forms a significant part of their training. The goal is for trainees to understand showroom furniture from the perspective of a designer, and to be able to translate that to the customer. By doing so, she says, associates will help buyers “make that connection between ‘designer led’ and our brand.”

Studio McGee's senior-level designers host regular check-ins with McGee & Co.’s design associates to help bridge the brand's designer-led vision.

For trade-focused businesses, trust-building exists outside of a single transaction. Tyla Caccese, the founder of the 15-year-old trade-only rug company Tailor-Made Textiles, emphasizes a practical tack. For her new 2,000-square-foot showroom in Manhattan, “We wanted it to feel more like a workshop,” she says. The design followed: There’s a big marble kitchen island where designers can spread out drawings, plug in their laptops, or work through a project over lunch.

This thinking was informed by her experiences in a shared space her brand occupied previously, where she noticed remote-working designers using the showroom as a kind of third place—not quite a home, not quite an office. “It’s been wonderful to see designers using the showroom almost as an extension of their own studios,” she says. These current and prospective customers can get to know and trust the brand through proximity and natural conversation, turning to Caccese to work through ideas and feel at home, whether or not they’re there to source a rug. “I don’t want designers to feel like they need a project or a purchase order to come through the door,” she says. Showing that you can help them solve their problems is what will earn you their business. “Ultimately, what brings designers back isn’t necessarily a particular rug. It’s knowing they can walk in with an idea, a problem, or a completely unrealistic deadline and have a real conversation about how to make something work.”

Once a customer makes a purchase, overcommunicate, overcommunicate, overcommunicate, says Lawson-Fenning co-founder Glenn Lawson. He says that wait times are the biggest challenge facing their business, which makes all their furniture to order. A piece can take 10 or 12 weeks to produce—and for a designer working toward an install date, that matters. “We’d rather give a realistic date and hit it than promise something faster and miss,” says Lawson. “When people know where their piece is, the wait feels shorter.” And in a pinch, those only-in-store items can help too: Never underestimate the power of a floor sample.

At the new ABC Carpet & Home store in Boca Raton, Florida, customers can explore the brand's floor coverings in a range of settings, from residential vignettes to more gallery-like arrangements.

Ultimately, retailers need to recognize that in 2026 and beyond, you’re no longer just a merchant—you’re a builder of relationships. That kinship builds through events that cultivate brand affinity, solving customers’ problems together, and delivering compelling, can’t-find-it-elsewhere in-store discovery. But nurturing that connection is just as important as making it in the first place.

“It’s not uncommon for our top buyers to receive a personal email from our sales team, letting them know about what we have coming up next and personally inviting them to check out new collections,” says Lennard. Fenning seconds the motion: “Designers hear about new work first,” he says. “We invite them in for a new collection or a maker’s show. And when a project wraps, we want to see the photos.” The transaction might end at the register—but the relationship doesn’t have to.

#4737. The BMW iX3 smashed its EPA range rating, driving well over 400 miles in a real-world test

BMW’s new iX3 outperformed the Volvo EX60 and Mercedes-Benz GLC EV, driving well over 400 miles during a real-world range test.

In a recent nationally representative survey, BMW found that Americans want more EV range than they actually need.

The study found that 73% consider 75 miles of range, or less, enough to cover their daily driving. Meanwhile, 42% said they would require at least 300 miles of range to consider an EV.

Another 53% said they would be more likely to consider an EV if it could add about 150 miles of range in 10 minutes.

BMW’s new iX3 checks all the boxes. Based on BMW’s sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive 800V system, the 2027 iX3 50 xDrive delivers an EPA-estimated range of up to 434 miles (with 20″ summer tires).

With the 22″ summer tires, the iX3 50 xDrive has an EPA-estimated range of up to 392 miles. Still, plenty for at least a week of commuting.

It can also add 170-185 miles of range in 10 minutes with up to 400 kW DC fast charging. In everyday, real-world driving, it may drive even further than its official EPA numbers suggest.

During Edmunds‘ EV Range test, the 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive (with 22″ summer tires) drove 436 miles on a single charge, topping its EPA estimate of 392 miles by 44 miles.

The electric SUV was also more efficient than advertised. The iX3 achieved an energy consumption of 28.3 kWh per 100 miles, beating its EPA estimate of 32 kWh per 100 miles by roughly 11.6%.

BMW’s new iX3 is now the longest-range luxury electric SUV that Edmunds has tested, outperforming rivals including the 2027 Volvo EX60 (352 miles) and Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric (392 miles).

The Edmunds real-world range test is designed to provide a more accurate estimate of an EV’s range in everyday driving conditions.

It consists of 60% city and 40% highway driving with an average speed of 40 mph. The vehicle stays within 5 mph of the posted speed limit, and the climate control is set to auto at 72 degrees.

The 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive is available to order in Sport, M Sport, and M Sport Professional trims, priced from $61,500, $64,000, and $65,500, respectively.

Average speed of 40 mph in perfect weather is an absolute best case scenario for EVs. I think cold weather 70 mph would be the worst case and it should be tested.

That said, I think BMW and Mercedes tend to underrate their cars published range (I think they publish worst case condition range). BMW iX and Mercedes have historically outperformed EPA ratings according to various articles and reddits posts.

But I think regardless of what we think of Edmunds tests, these are some crazy range figures and with roughly 100kwh usable battery capacity, you are still looking at close to 4 miles per kwh. As an example across the Ultium platform anything from Chevy or Cadillac barely breaches 300 miles. The big Escalade and pickup trucks have 225+ kwh battery so I am not counting them.

If the depreciation rate for luxury EVs holds up, in 2-3 years, they will be awesome value.

Powered by a 108.7 kWh battery, the new iX3 with 20″ Summer Tires delivers up to 434 miles of range on a single charge.

With a charging rate of up to 400 kW, the new BMW iX3 can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 21 minutes, or add about 185 miles in 10 minutes.

Inside, the electric SUV features the Neue Klasse interior design. The setup includes BMW’s new Panoramic Vision, a full-length windshield display, and a 17.9″ central infotainment screen running the latest Operating System X. Buyers can also upgrade to the optional BMW 3D Head-Up Display.

#4736. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Not Be Linked to Colorectal Cancer

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Ultra-processed foods as a group do not increase the risk of colorectal cancer, according to a new study.

Researchers from the National Cancer Institute (NCI) report that they found no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and colorectal cancer incidence among the more than 400,000 adults they studied.

They said their findings are important because ultra-processed foods now account for more than half of adults’ energy intake in the United States. They published their research on October 15 in PLOS Medicine.

The study comes amid recent research that has connected ultra-processed foods to an increased risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity.

However, the link between colorectal cancer and ultra-processed foods has been less clear.

A 2025 study reported that ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of colorectal cancer in females under 50.

A 2022 study found that males who consumed high rates of ultra-processed foods had a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer.

NCI scientists noted in their new study that ultra-processed products represent a wide range of foods.

They pointed out that foods such as whole grains and dairy products were associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer among study participants, while foods such as processed meats were associated with a higher risk.

“We did not observe an association between total ultra-processed food (UPF) intake and colorectal cancer incidence,” said Erikka Loftfield, PhD, a former investigator with the NCI, in a news release. “However, when we looked at food groups, like whole grains, dairy, and meat, by UPF or non-UPF source, we found that associations were in line with current dietary guidance for colorectal cancer prevention.”

Experts not involved in the study told Healthline that the NCI scientists appear to be on the right track.

“While the study did not find that overall ultra-processed food intake was associated with colorectal cancer risk, the findings suggest that simply classifying foods by their level of processing may not tell the whole story,” said Marissa Shams-White, PhD, a senior principal scientist in population science at the American Cancer Society.

“One of the challenges with studying ultra-processed foods is that the category includes a very wide range of foods and beverages, and we don’t yet know whether they all relate to colorectal cancer risk in the same way,” she added.

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, agrees.

“Just because it is ultra-processed doesn’t mean it is inherently bad or good for you,” he said. “The source of the food and the additives like preservatives, flavorings, sugars, and pigments that are added to increase palatability probably play a much larger role in increasing cancer risk.”

“A whole grain cereal and a hot dog are both UPF, but they push risk in opposite directions,” Thanki noted.

In their study, the National Cancer Institute researchers analyzed data from 461,682 adults aged 50 to 71 years who enrolled in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study between 1995 and 1996.

The participants recorded their eating habits using a food frequency questionnaire. Researchers then used that data to estimate each person’s intake of ultra-processed foods. The median consumption of ultra-processed foods among participants was 43% of daily median intake.

The participants were then followed until 2018, for a median of nearly 19 years. The scientists reported that 10,075 cases of colorectal adenocarcinoma were diagnosed during that period.

The researchers reported no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and the incidence of colorectal cancer.

However, they said their findings varied by food type. Higher intake of whole grains, fiber, dairy products, and calcium derived from UPF sources was associated with lower colorectal cancer incidence, while meat from UPF sources was associated with higher incidence.

Researchers also found that replacing 10% of gram weight from UPF intake with minimally processed foods was associated with a 2% lower incidence of CRC.

The researchers acknowledged limitations to their study.

They noted that the participants were primarily older, white Americans. In addition, UPF intake was only measured once at the beginning of the study period, so the findings cannot account for changes in eating habits or the increasing availability of ultra-processed foods.

Nonetheless, Ashkan Farhadi, MD, a gastroenterologist at MemorialCare Orange Coast Medical Center in California, who wasn’t involved in the study, said he found the results “very interesting.”

“The definition of ultra-processed foods is so broad,” he told Healthline. “It’s important to designate what type of ultra-processed foods you’re talking about.”

“You shouldn’t just go by whether a food is designated as ultra-processed,” Farhadi added. “You should go by what’s on the [ingredient] label.”

Shams-White shared a similar approach. “When it comes to diet, it is important to follow an overall healthy dietary pattern,” she told Healthline. “Emphasize a variety of fruits and vegetables and whole grains and limit red and processed meats, sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-processed foods, and refined grain products.”

“Eating a diet rich in fiber and whole grains, dairy and calcium, and limiting processed and red meat and alcohol is what really reduces your risk of developing cancer,” added Thanki.

The American Cancer Society estimates there will be about 108,000 new cases of colon cancer and nearly 50,000 new cases of rectal cancer in the United States in 2026.

The incidence rate is slightly higher in men than in females.

The organization reports that the rate of colorectal cancer cases in the United States has declined since the mid-1980s, but they note that most of that decrease has occurred in older adults.

The incidence rate among people under 50 increased by nearly 3% from 2013 to 2022. Colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of death from cancer for U.S. adults under the age of 50.

Colorectal cancer occurs when cells in the large intestine grow out of control. About 70% of cases begin in the colon.

There are a number of symptoms of colorectal cancer. Some of the common ones include:

Diet is considered one of the risk factors for colorectal cancer. However, there are other considerations.

Farhadi said genetics, obesity, smoking, alcohol consumption, and a sedentary lifestyle can also increase a person’s risk of developing colorectal cancer.

Shams-White noted that the American Cancer Society Guideline for Diet and Physical Activity for Cancer Prevention recommended achieving and maintaining a healthy weight, being physically active, following a healthy eating pattern, and avoiding alcohol and tobacco.

Thanki points out that there are risk factors for colorectal cancer that can be modified and others that can’t.

“Among non-modifiable factors, the biggest are age, a personal or family history of colorectal cancer or advanced polyps, inherited syndromes such as Lynch syndrome, and longstanding inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s colitis),” he told Healthline.

“On the modifiable side, the evidence is strongest for obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, alcohol, and diets high in red and processed meat and low in fiber, whole grains, and calcium,” he added.

Colorectal cancer treatment outcomes improve if the disease is caught at an early stage. The 5-year relative survival for localized colorectal cancer is 91.3%. The 5-year relative survival rate for colorectal cancer caught at various stages, including cancer that has spread, is 65.4%.

Shams-White points out that the American Cancer Society Colorectal Cancer Guidelines recommend that people at average risk of colorectal cancer start getting screened at age 45.

“Screening can help prevent cancer by finding abnormal cells and polyps so they can be removed before they can become colorectal cancer, as well as detect cancer at an earlier stage,” she said.

Thanki had similar advice. “Get screened starting at 45, or earlier if you have a family history or other risk factors, because colonoscopies can prevent cancer by removing polyps,” he said. “And never ignore symptoms like rectal bleeding or a change in bowel habits at any age.”

Compared to other oud-forward scents, this one is both identifiable as oud (i.e., elegant and sexy) but isn’t so overpowering that it’s going to leave a scent trail wherever you go.

A lot is written about Dior Sauvage, and rightfully so—it’s a dark, spicy scent that leaves a serious impression. But much of that hype overshadows the best, most masculine Dior scent: Homme. Dior Homme Parfum takes the classic scent I love and gives it a bolder, woodsy, amber twist that’s built for this chilly weather. The iris at its core feels smooth and modern—soft yet strong—balanced by warm, ambery woods that linger long after the first spray. It hits harder and lasts longer than the original Homme without losing that signature sophistication. Even the bottle reflects its power: sleek, heavy, and designed to look as refined as it smells.

Inspired by a garden after the rain, this new take on freshness leans heavy on the green and skips the citrus, which can overpower its subtle vibe. A hint of juicy pear adds light sweetness and a cooling effect that amplifies it. It also features a note called physcool, which is a chill, minty accord that reacts with the moisture on your skin to create a zingy tingle that drives home the fresh vibe. The result is a modern, versatile scent that works anywhere and on every guy.

I’ve never passed the folks playing chess in Washington Square Park and thought, “Man, I’d love to smell like those dudes.” But the strategy and tension of the game somehow inspired one of my favorite emerging fragrance houses, Mind Games. Its best release to date, Opera Mate, swaps checkmates for curtain calls, channeling the drama of the Paris Opera House into scent form. To me, it smells like a grand finale—elegant, layered, and impossible to ignore.

Opera Mate pulls me in from the first spray with creamy sandalwood and a touch of caramel that melt together into smooth, golden warmth. As it opens, roasted chestnut and grapefruit give it a lift, like a spark before the curtain rises. Then it deepens, revealing rich suede, smoky vetiver, and resinous benzoin that linger on the skin. It feels elegant yet bold, the kind of scent that commands attention without shouting. I wear it when I want to smell like confidence with a touch of drama.

This bottle is a loud, vibrant green reminiscent of Vulcan blood, which is fitting because it’s the logical choice for anyone looking for a refined, interesting scent. The scent itself is amber-woody, sure, but it’s a little spicy and bold without being obnoxious.

It opens with warm, resinous notes of Peru balsam, benzoin, and guaiac wood before evolving into green Bourbon geranium with rosy facets, while bergamot and musk add a fresh lift. It’s a collection of notes that feels like they shouldn’t work, but together create something powerful and new—one of those scents that’s hard to place in a single fragrance family.

When you think of aquatic scents, you typically think of notes like citrus, driftwood, and salty notes that mimic seawater. This surprising cologne, however, flips that idea on its head. Inspired by the Adriatic islands, there are notes of olive oil, fig, pine needles, cypress, and wild herbs. You still have a wet, oceanic quality that gives it an aquatic nature, but without citrus, the effect is earthier and more grounded, not to mention long-lasting and way more sophisticated. If you love fresh colognes but want to elevate your game, this one is for you.

Look, I get why the OG Bleu de Chanel is a classic fragrance; its blend of grapefruit, cedar, and sandalwood hits that sweet spot of being masculine without feeling like it’s begging for attention. But over the past couple of years since Bleu de Chanel L'Exclusif was released—and named a 2026 Men’s Health Grooming Award winner—I found myself wearing it far more often.

It’s darker and denser, with much more staying power. The original Bleu de Chanel felt like a crisp summer morning, bright and fresh, whereas L'Exclusif is more like a windy, layered fall evening. It maintains some of the citrusy freshness of the original before evolving into something deeper, with sandalwood, leathery cistus labdanum, and woody amber notes taking over. It’s intense, aromatic, and guaranteed to make a statement.

While I love eating vanilla-flavored things (mostly ice cream, if I’m being honest), I was never a huge fan of the scent. This 2026 Men’s Health Grooming Award-winning cologne changed that for me—it’s easily the best vanilla fragrance I’ve worn. Don’t let the name fool you; the vanilla here isn’t the strongest note.

This cologne has a deep, leathery suede base layered with rich labdanum and amber notes for a masculine, cozy scent that’s perfect for cooler weather. The vanilla is just enough to spice things up from my usual leathery or amber colognes, but it doesn’t overpower the core of the fragrance. It’s strong too. A couple of sprays on my neck in the morning lasts me ten hours. Best part? It’s only $82. For a cologne of this quality, you usually have to spend at least twice that.

Read More: 2026 Men’s Health Grooming Awards

I’ve always loved the smell of campfire smoke; the deep, woody burn that clings to your clothes and stays in your memory. City on Fire captures this feeling better than any cologne I’ve ever tried, and I wear it year-round—bold in winter, magnetic in summer. It opens with spicy black pepper and dark berries before revealing layers of cardamom, labdanum, and clearwood that flicker like embers. The scent of cade oil and burnt match adds a rugged, smoldering edge that feels both primal and sophisticated.

Like all Imaginary Authors fragrances, it’s built around a story—in this case, a noir-like tale about two matchmakers drawn together by murder and mystery—and that narrative energy inspires the scent’s smoky, cinematic depth. I love how it lingers for hours, shifting from bright heat to soft ash, like the last glow of a fire you never want to leave. To be clear, this stuff is strong. If you’re not a fan of smoky fragrances, you’ll want to look elsewhere. But if you do dig a smoky cologne, this will quickly become a favorite.

Fragrance families are your roadmap to finding the right cologne. Once you figure out which group you’re drawn to, narrowing your search gets a whole lot easier. The four main families—fresh, floral, woody, and amber—cover almost every scent on the market, though some blends straddle more than one. You might also see fougère listed as a fifth family, but we treat it as a note within the woody category. Here’s how the big four break down:

Be it of the top, heart, or base variety, scent notes are far more specific than fragrance families, often referring to individual scent ingredients or aromas that make up a fragrance. The foundational notes of men’s cologne rarely change, but fragrance chemists (real thing!) are always updating the classics to build younger scents (also a thing!) that smell more modern. Of course, there are many more, but some key notes you’ll find in our favorite colognes are:

The eternal question when faced with purchasing any self-care product is what size to buy. When it comes to cologne, there are a few factors to keep in mind that’ll determine how big or small you’ll want to go here. For one, how often do you plan to wear the cologne? If you plan to make this your new daily scent, buy a bigger bottle so it’ll last longer.

But if you’re merely testing a fragrance or looking for something seasonal, consider a smaller option. Not to mention, cologne can run a bit expensive, especially for some of the stronger versions. So remember that buying a larger container can often offset some of the cost.

Cologne is personal, and what smells incredible on one guy might be missed entirely on another. That’s why the Men’s Health grooming team has been testing and debating scents nonstop since this story first ran in 2020. Over the years, we’ve sprayed, worn, and ranked hundreds of colognes across every fragrance family, taking notes on how they apply, evolve, and hold up through the day.

For this updated guide, I revisited our past favorites, compared them with new releases, and leaned on expert feedback to narrow it all down. Below, you’ll find the ten best colognes for men that are timeless, modern, and made to work in every season.

Apply cologne to the places where you can feel the beats of your heart. This means wrists, the sides of your neck, and over your ticker. The throb adds impact to the scent.

No cologne is perfect for every person, but there are a few best practices to follow when testing a new scent to find the right fit for you. For starters, don't bombard your skin with too many scents. When testing colognes, stick to no more than three on your skin so you can clearly tell each scent apart, says fragrance developer Ann Gottlieb.

So be selective with which you want to trial when browsing in-store because, as Gottlieb warns, testing too many too quickly can lead to nose fatigue. Gottlieb also recommends allowing a scent to linger on you for at least 30 minutes before deciding to buy. This lets you see how a fragrance reacts and develops with your own, unique body chemistry.

BMW introduced a new public charging package for those who buy or lease the new 2027 iX3, i5, or i7 electric vehicles.

BMW’s electric vehicle lineup will look much different in 2027. The German luxury automaker is shaking things up with the arrival of its Neue Klasse EVs, bringing significantly longer ranges, faster charging times, and advanced new tech and features.

To sweeten the deal, BMW launched a new public charging promotion on Thursday for eligible model-year 2027 electric vehicles, including the new iX3, i5, and i7.

The new BMW ChargingNetwork package provides $500 in total credits. $300 of which includes a BMW ChargingNetwork credit that can be used at one of 15 public charging providers, such as ChargePoint, EVgo, Shell Recharge, and IONNA. The other $200 is for IONNA locations only.

On top of this, the promo includes a free one-year BMW Membership at IONNA. The membership provides a 25% discount on charging during the free year trial.

BMW said the charging credits will automatically apply after you enroll in the BMW ChargingNetwork.

You can enroll through the My BMW app. Under Charging, select Services, then Charging Wallet, and then BMW ChargingNetwork. Once complete, the credits and other benefits will show up in the Digital Charging Wallet and will be automatically applied to eligible charging sessions.

Which one to choose? The 2027 iX3 is BMW’s first Neue Klasse vehicle. Based on its sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive, the iX3 delivers an EPA-estimated range of up to 434 miles.

Inside, it features BMW’s revamped Neue Klasse interior design. The setup includes the new BMW Panoramic Vision, a full-length display spanning the base of the windshield, and a large 17.9″ infotainment screen running the latest BMW Operating System X.

Meanwhile, the 2027 i5, which still offers up to 310 miles of range, is not built on the dedicated Neue Klasse platform.

As part of a mid-cycle refresh, it adopts BMW’s new style but lacks some Neue Klasse tech and features found on the iX3 and i7.

In the first quarter of 2027, BMW will launch the new iX5 and i3. Both are based on the Neue Klasse platform.

#4732. After Launching McGee & Co., Shea McGee Shares 8 Lessons for Opening a Store

My husband Syd and I are both lovers of retail, and have always known one day we’d have a McGee & Co. shop of our own. Over the years, we’ve spent a lot of time jotting down ideas for our own store. Our new flagship is a repository for all that knowledge that we’ve been squirreling away—but it also taught us a few lessons of its own.

Speaking to you now, on the other side of its debut, there are some things we only learned through actually doing. From the importance of developing a training manual to the do-or-die value of a soft launch, here are eight hard-won learnings from our McGee & Co. store launch.

It was important to us that the shop feel like the homes we create for our clients—layered and collected, with a variety of patterns and objects for your eye to explore. Despite the fact that the dollars-per-square-foot model is the traditional method of conceiving an in-store assortment, it was more important for us to remain true to ourselves with this first location: we’re a designer-led brand, not a merchant-led one.

“I’m getting to see our products through new eyes—and I was the one that concepted them!” says Shea. “When you see them in a store setting, pieces can have a lot more detail than you can see online.”

We started by coming up with the sections we envisioned, like a kids’ area, a kitchen zone, and so on. Then we created planograms to see how much we could actually fit, and reconciled with our merchandising team to see what made business sense. Sometimes, that meant pivoting from the early vision. A lighting gallery we had planned, for instance, ended up shifting: We loved the idea, but when we looked at the percentage of lighting to the rest of our sales, we could see clearly that it was a smarter business decision to use this space to showcase more furniture. Instead of the sprawling lighting gallery we had imagined, we created a moody lounge area that can flex to showcase different pieces.

We don’t think small: Our aspirations are to grow nationwide. But however much we scale, it’s critical that we not lose the warm, personal feeling that comes from a standalone store. As McGee & Co. grows its brick-and-mortar operation, that’s one of my biggest goals. And there’s another layer here, too: Being a personality-led business, the team members in our store aren’t just representing our brand—they’re representing me, for better or worse. The design world can sometimes feel closed-off and unapproachable, and it’s always been the McGee mantra—in our content, in our personality on social media, in how we work with clients—to be warm and accessible. Now that attitude needs to trickle down to our store associates, too.

Before we opened, I spent months developing a comprehensive training guide for our associates. It’s essentially Design 101, McGee-style, covering everything from how many inches I place a rug away from a wall, to how to pair and arrange accent tables, to how to layer bedding. We cover every level of the decorating process. Thank goodness for AI—it’s been a lifesaver: I’ll narrate as we go on our walk-throughs, and use those notes as the basis for the training manual. And it’s not a one-and-done deal. We’ll continue to add to this document as we evolve and grow.

Every issue, every era. Explore 100+ years of the Architectural Digest Archive, an unparalleled digital resource for research and inspiration. Start Searching

Having that Design 101 established is a first step, but how do you ensure that the team is really internalizing the lessons? For us, the answer was checkpoints. As our design associates go through training and familiarize themselves with our ways of doing things, we hold check-ins with them to make sure that they’re absorbing our ways of operating. It’s the exact same as we do for the junior interior designers at Studio McGee: The checkpoints allow us to build up mutual confidence, with the aim for them to eventually fly on their own.

Shea plans to have the studio’s senior-level designers hosting regular check-ins with the shop’s design associates.

Personally dropping in myself can serve as another kind of checkpoint, too. With the flagship local, I’m able to stop by regularly in these early days to make sure that our standards are upheld, that our visuals are tight, and the operation is humming. That won’t work for us in every location, but it’s certainly a perk of opening up in our own hometown.

As much as I love a good plan, there’s nothing like real-time feedback to show you what’s working and what’s not. Which is why we kicked off our flagship back in September with a whisper and not a bang. We did a very soft launch with no announcement, no social post. We just opened the doors. As folks wandered in, we learned, and we tweaked. And two weeks later, we opened officially. That soft-launch period was vital for us in getting the kinks out.

One benefit of having had an ecommerce business for so long is that we have rich data on exactly where our customers are. That means that from day one, we already know where we need to open next. While launching in Salt Lake City was a logical place for our flagship, we’re already thinking ahead to how we’ll expand to some of our other biggest markets, like Texas and California.

Located in Salt Lake City’s Trolley Square, the “shop,” as Shea calls it, is 7,500 square feet.

We want to capitalize on the fact that the retail-ecommerce loop is an advantageous cycle: Where you have a retail store, your ecommerce sales lift. People who are aware of your product can go see it in person, give it a sit test, think about it, and then finish the sale online. In store, we can educate them, give them styling suggestions, and show off the quality of the product in ways we can’t online. Even for us, we’re discovering new things about our assortment by merchandising it in the store—we’re seeing it with fresh eyes, and we know our customers will too.

Aside from the obvious metric of profitability, to me, success in these early days means nailing down our systems and processes. It’s not the most glamorous side of this business, but it’s a must. I want to be able to say that we know what it takes to run a store and to make the shopper experience in it as smooth as possible. For instance, I want customers to know how to get to our free design services, and to have a great experience using them. If we can do that, we know we’re on our way to some of our loftier goals, too.

I’m not under any illusions here: This first store is a baptism by fire. Not only are we opening a flagship and planting seeds for our future locations—we’re also doing it in Q4, right before the holidays. But my hope is that at the end of it, we can catch our breath and take a moment to reflect on what worked, what didn’t, and then get to work fixing it. In this business, honesty with yourself is the only way up.

“The kitchen is a working kitchen,” says Shea, who envisions cooking demos and community events enlivening the space.
