"The key features you want to look for are weight, dimension, and material," Johns tells Men's Health. Once you know this is a sport for you, here is what he mentions when making that investment buy. "The right time to buy a paddle is usually when you find yourself wanting to improve your skills as a player, as opposed to just playing for fun every now and then."

With the help of Johns (as well as other experts) and a ton of our own testing, we'll outline what to look for when buying a pickleball paddle and detail why these are the best ones we've found.

DOWNLOAD OUR ULTIMATE PICKLEBALL WORKOUT PLAN PDF

When it comes to pickleball, Selkirk leads the way with its fantastic lineup of paddles, and its LUXX Control paddle just may be its most polished yet. At the end of the day, controlling your shot and placing the ball exactly where you want it to go reigns king, and this paddle does that best.

This midweight paddle strikes a balance between high-tech specs and craftsmanship, featuring a slightly longer frame (16.45 inches) and a lengthy handle (5.35 inches), which allows for greater reach and more room to perform a two-handed backhand. The Florek carbon fiber face and thick 20mm honeycomb core provide the accuracy you need without compromising your ability to generate powerful shots.

Having the pleasure of playing with this paddle, I just love the way that it seamlessly cuts through the air. Unlike other cheaper paddles that can create drag, this one does not. It almost feels like my reflexes are quicker when I play with it.

This paddle just does it all, from its modern looks to its accurate shot placements to the power and speed it can create—there's nothing this paddle can't do. With a presence for controlled hits, each shot feels intentional, while still maximizing power. While it may lack the elite pop of others, its overall performance outshines that drawback. With its current reduced price, it's hard to beat, making it our pick for the best overall pickleball paddle.

Head's Radical Elite paddle is the ultimate wallet-friendly pick for those who are getting pickleball fever. As far as design goes, the Radical Elite comes with a honeycomb core, a fiberglass finish, and a wide surface area to smack the ball. You also get a comfortable foam handle with a length similar to that of a tennis racket.

While the Radical Elite lacked power a bit, this paddle prioritizes control while staying lightweight, so it's a great option for learning the game. You can play competitively with the Radical Elite too, but as you see yourself progressing you may want to switch to a paddle with more power. But remember, this paddle retails for around $50, when in reality it plays closer to a $100 paddle. It's such a good price that it makes for an easy pickleball gift you can give to players of all skill levels (experts can use it as a backup paddle).

Made in collaboration with Ben Johns, who has dominated the PPA tour for years, having won an impressive 123 title wins. This paddle is made with enhanced stability, giving you a precise shot from its charged carbon surface. Basically, it’s been bond-treated for improved strength, which gives you a crisp feel during contact for improved energy return on the ball. In a nutshell, this gives you a “poppier” response.

What helps make this one pro-level paddle is the insane propulsion core. It’s designed with a patent-pending core that gives you explosive power unlike any other, on all shots, from line drives, drops, dinks, and counters. Combine that with an elongated paddle face, and you will have ample hitting surface area to make you a spin master with an enormous "sweet spot," meaning fewer miss hits, too. One of the best features is that this paddle is NFC chip-enabled. In a world where data is king, this allows you to access training vids based on your style of play, a community experience, and gamification, all through the JOOLA Connect app. This thing truly is next level.

A $250 pickleball paddle is no easy investment, but those who want premium gear will find the Selkirk Power Air Epic interesting. But it’s no longer regularly priced, and has gotten discounts over the years (it can currently be had between $120 to $187 depending on the website). One of the elite models on the PPA tour, this is one "epic" paddle. For starters, the Power Air has an elongated handle and stand shape that creates a generous surface area, while the handle makes it perfect for double-handed backhands. Second, the Power Air’s performance is some of the most advanced—it’s truly a power player's dream. Selkirk added the air opening to create faster swing speeds, as it feels like serves have some extra whip to them.

A third key finding from playing with the Power Air Epic was the overall feel of the paddle. It's like holding the paddle equivalent of a Ferrari: fast, lightweight, sexy. The handle is luxe and cushioned, and the extra wrapping near the end of the handle helps you get a more secure grip. There are no pronounced edges on the Power Air for the ball to take a weird shot off of, so there's actually a chance you get a clean return even if you connect near the edges of the paddle.

The Power Air Epic is meant for serious players only (and the price tag reflects that), and the sleek design shows that you're using the best technology in the game.

If you watch any professional pickleball events on TV, it's likely you'll notice Onix as a paddle in a few pro's hands. Onix has a wide array of paddles to choose from, but the Graphite Z5 is a trusted pick that's big on ball control and clean returns. The takeaway from the Z5 is that you get the best qualities of a graphite paddle for a price point of just under $100, which is an excellent value. Graphite is a favorite for many pros due to the material's strong design and lightweight feel, making it easy to control each shot and finesse where you want your ball to go.

It plays with a well-balanced feeling in the hand. The Nomex honeycomb core seems to limit dead spots, and the paddle offers enough space to connect cleanly on most shots. (The shape of the paddle gives you a sneaky amount of surface area, too.) In terms of quality, the paddle has a lofty weight and powerful sweet spot, giving it a superior rating. The paddle was especially great on serves, allowing you to whip the ball over the net and get some good spin. The Z5 caters to all skill levels, but it's especially great as a beginner pickleball paddle—you won't have to upgrade from it for quite a while.

Once you've played the game long enough and can consider yourself an advanced player, you need a paddle that demands more than just control. You need a paddle that can deliver heavy line drives, insane spin, and provide all the pop and power you can imagine. That is exactly what you get in the SLK Era Power paddle.

Its fusion core is a blend of polypropylene honeycomb surrounded by EVA foam, increasing its overall stability and taking its forgiveness to another level—something you don't find too often in a power paddle. I love that even when I miss the sweet spot on a hit, it still feels stable in my hand, which means I can worry less about having to make perfect contact each time. A rare thing for elongated paddles.

Its elongated shape, measuring 16.5 inches with a 5.8-inch handle, provides great reach on every shot and ample space for double-backhands. Combined with its three-layer face of fiberglass and T700 raw carbon fiber, shots on this paddle seem to jump off its surface (according to Selkirk's website, this paddle can generate speeds up to 2,000 rpm). This paddle is excellent for aggressive players.

While its price may be a bit of an investment, and there is a bit of a learning curve with elongated paddles like this, its overall performance easily outweighs those setbacks, especially for advanced players. If you're seeking a pro-level paddle that swings well, puts ample pop on each shot, and looks good doing it, the SLK Era Power is for you.

For those looking to put their shots on "spin cycle," the Quartz paddle from Six Zero is for you. The face of the paddle is crafted from raw textured T300 carbon which gives it the perfect hitting surface for maximum traction on the ball. Translation: more rpm and way more spin. Then, you also have the lightweight design, allowing for way faster swings and quick hands, which again can translate to more revolutions on the ball. Not only does it give you top-tier spin, but it has a great flexibility to give you good control over your shot placements, too.

It has a solidly large sweet spot for shot forgiveness, and thanks to its one-piece unibody construction, it was also designed with durability in mind. For a paddle that is performance-driven and for a price under $100, this is one of the best paddles on our list. They also have multiple pops of color that wrap around the head of the paddle and really stand out on the blacked-out face, so there’s a choice for everyone, too.

If you want a nice and wide paddle for maximal surface area, the Project Boomstik in the widebody model is the way to go. So, why would you want a wider paddle if it means a slower swing speed? Well for starters, widebodies are great for forgiveness and minimizing mishits. The Project Boomstik gives you a generous sweet spot and is a perfect choice for those who love to work the net in the kitchen (where the game is truly won and lost).

With this Selkirk model, you get a nice and long handle too, which makes it an even greater choice for defensive players who prioritize paddle and ball control. And even though most would consider this a defensive player’s choice, it’s loaded with Selkirk’s BoomCore tech to help give it plenty of pop on all your power shots. Plus, it makes for one heck of a durable paddle.

While it is arguably one of the most expensive off-the-rack models you can buy, if you wanna dominate the competition, even as a rookie, this one will get the job done.

The one paddle that I have been [patiently] waiting to get my hands on is this highly anticipated Honeyfoam TKO-X model, which builds on the brand’s super successful Reserve special edition model. At the heart of its build is the proprietary three-foam design that gives it even more energy return delivering excellent power on every shot. The ball jumps off the surface, so much so that it took a couple of points for me to adjust (but in a good way). Once I got it figured out, my opponent was left scrambling to return my aggressive forehands. Its advanced edge guard also dampens shock quite well, no matter how much power I put into it.

But, it’s not all power no touch either, as I could easily control shots in the kitchen as well, making it a surprisingly well-rounded paddle. This is partially thanks to its elongated design, which makes those hard-to-reach shots just that much easier. While it is one of the most expensive options in our guide, its soft touch and great power make this my new favorite competitive paddle.

If you’re looking for a paddle to make a statement on the courts and one that can easily fit in at a country club, Modest Vintage Player is that paddle. Its pro heritage model aesthetic is one inspired by the brand’s exceptional work with leather. It’s also perfectly complemented with a carbon fiber head, which ensures this pick is more than just a pretty paddle, as it performs quite well, too.

With a generous sweet spot and slightly oversized face, this paddle is a great choice for players of all levels, which helps you maintain optimal control. It weighs 8.6 ounces, which means you also get plenty of power on shots when you whip around on your strokes. The 4K weave carbon fiber surface gives it a nice responsive pop while the paddle's thickness perfectly balances accuracy and power. The slick blacked-out face perfectly matches the chestnut brown leather grip. Plus, with its air scoop design, you get the feel of a pro-level paddle for half the cost, yet this one gives you all the heritage vibes you could want.

The average weight for a paddle is going to be around 8 ounces and fluctuates above and below that number. Anything at 9 ounces is usually too heavy and anything under 7 ounces is usually too light. "For weight, somewhere in between 7.5 to 8.3 ounces is a good range," says Johns.

The basic configuration most new players will want to use is called a "wide body paddle" according to Carl Schmits, Managing Director of Equipment Standards & Facilities Development for the USA Pickleball Association. "This configuration is easiest to maneuver and is also good for a controlled, more defensive style of play. Paddles that are close to 8 inches wide by 16 inches long are within the wide body category," says Schmits. "Players that have well-developed stroke mechanics from other sports may be most comfortable with paddles having a longer shape (between 16" and a maximum of 17") and some with a longer handle will better facilitate two-handed backhands, which is an increasingly common grip used very successfully by tennis converts."

Carbon fiber and fiberglass composites are the two most common materials used in high-quality paddles, as they have been shown to help players deliver speed and spin on the ball. A good pickleball paddle should also have zero dead spots, meaning when you make a quality hit on the ball it doesn't randomly underperform and fall flat. "When it comes to the material, I like to look for a polypropylene core with a fiberglass or carbon fiber face," says Johns.

Similar to how you might shop for a driver in golf, your pickleball paddle is going to have a formula of power and control that works for you. A power paddle will have a tight sweet spot and deliver a shot with more pop, while a control paddle has a larger sweet spot that's softer but allows for more consistent returns.

For a power paddle, look for something tighter and more compact in all areas of the design."Paddles that have thinner cores, like a 13mm-14mm, have longer configuration, and typically made with fiberglass faces will return more power, although hitting the ball with heat is as much a result of an efficient kinetic chain as anything," says Schmits.

If you want a paddle with more control, a design with maneuverable dimensions and a carbon fiber face (as opposed to a fiberglass face, which is harder) is recommended. "I'd look for at least 8 inches of width on the paddle head and for a thicker core that's 16 millimeters or more, or 5/8 inches or more," says Johns.

Our experts explained to us grip circumference carries just as much importance in a pickleball paddle as it does in a tennis racket. They also noted there are fewer options when it comes to shopping for specific grip sizes for pickleball (most brands use a standard 4.25" size). Most pickleball paddle grips will vary from just under 4" and no bigger than 5.5".

John Crowley Sr., the Sr. Category Merchandising Manager of Paddles at Pickleball Central, recommends starting with a smaller grip first (when picking between two paddles) and then adding an overgrip if needed. "Very few manufacturers offer different grip sizes and materials, so customizing with an overgrip wrap is the best way to build up the grip to a comfortable size," added Schmits.

A reliable pickleball paddle is usually thick, as brands fill the interior space with their own technology to limit the odds of any dead spots. One popular interior makeup is a polypropylene core (also called honeycomb core design) which is a type of interior webbing that's made into a honeycomb shape to ensure the paddle is evenly balanced.

I have been fortunate enough to play with numerous paddles over the past couple of years, from multi-hundred-dollar paddles to those under $50, and I can tell you that it’s not always about the cost that makes a paddle worth playing with. Through my time playing regularly and testing gear along the way, I've combined that experience along with paddle recommendations from the Men's Health editors and writers who also play consistently. For this guide, we considered everything when we compiled our list of recommendations, including weight, dimension, material, grip circumference, core design, aesthetics, feel, and price. Once I gathered all our notes, I compared paddles based on performance and durability. We also considered what paddles appeal best to specific skill levels, from beginners to 4.0-rated players.

After testing tons of different pickleball paddles and consulting with experts, we eventually landed on 10 pickleball paddles we recommend for 2026.

Just like shopping for running shoes, you can find pickleball paddles at all types of prices. Generally speaking, expect to pay anywhere from $60 to $100 for a beginner- to intermediate-level paddle. If you're looking for an advanced paddle, any model we recommend above $100 is a worthy choice.

If you're going to play more than two times a month, Johns says it's time to invest in a paddle: "The right time to upgrade your paddle is usually when you find yourself wanting to improve your skills as a player as opposed to just playing for fun every now and then."

Crowley Sr. also gave us tips on how to go about investing in a paddle. "When you go shopping have a budget in mind (the best value to price is no object). How much do you plan to play? What is your sports background and if you know, what style of player are you—power player, control player, or all court?" he says.

If you think you have to splurge on a competition-ready paddle, think again. "I say shoot for the $75 to $100 range for your first paddle if you want to play competitively," says Laura Gainor, USA Pickleball's Director of Media Relations. "And if you’re planning to sign up for your first tournament, make sure your paddle is USA Pickleball approved." We agree there's nothing worse than bringing your paddle to a match and discovering you need to find a different one that complies with the rules.

Fiberglass and graphite paddles have characteristics about them that can play to your natural strengths on the court. "You are trying to find the recipe that works best for you," says Crowley Sr.

In general, fiberglass pickleball paddles have more power but less control than a graphite paddle. This is mainly due to the fact fiberglass weighs more. Graphite, on the other hand, is lighter and stronger due to the thinly layered construction of the material. Graphite paddles are often associated with better control, resulting in a better ability to place each return where you want it.

Fiberglass paddles are more wallet-friendly, and have been gaining in popularity due to their quality performance while staying at a good price point. Graphite paddles are more expensive and are often seen being used more by pros in tournaments.

One other paddle material to consider is composite. For example, you might find a composite design that incorporates carbon fiber and fiberglass in hopes of bringing equal parts control and power. Composite paddles are usually high quality and exist at graphite-level prices (or higher), but it's important to make sure the paddle is USA Pickleball approved if you ever want to play competitively.

While all of the paddles above were curated with attention to sweet spot, there are a few characteristics you can prioritize when shopping.

The first is to go by surface area. You will probably get the most sizable sweet spot area by going off the most common dimension of a 16" length and 8" width paddle. Second is inner material of the paddle: look for a trusted core material, like a honeycomb propylene core design, that can cover all areas of the paddle and help reduce the chance of there being any dead spots.

Last is the type of material used to construct the paddle. There are a lot of fiberglass paddles out there with generous sweet spots, but if you want to get the largest sweet spot possible then going to a more expensive graphite paddle is probably the best move.

There are two situations where you want to consider replacing your paddle. The first is if you find yourself playing more (and perhaps more competitively) than when you first started. A good rule of thumb is if you're playing more than two times a month, it's probably time to consider investing in a competitive play paddle.

The second situation that would warrant replacing your paddle is if it's damaged or worn down from constant play. If you stick to the paddles we recommend above, you can expect the lifespan to last between 1 to 3 years. But sometimes your paddle can wear out faster (also called a "dead paddle") if you're playing much more. In order to tell if you need to replace your paddle due to overuse, pay attention to the feel and how the ball comes off the paddle. Is it returning or serving shots the same way it was in the first few months of use? If not, your paddle is probably wearing down.

You can also pay attention to the sound of the ball off the paddle. Are your best shots delivering a nice and clear pop? Or are they sounding flat and droopy? If you're out playing consistently, then you will probably know when your paddle is ready for retirement.

Pickleball paddles are resilient. They can take a beating on the court, but off the court you should keep them away from the sun and heat for extended periods of time.

If you're concerned about keeping your paddle pristine-looking, invest in a paddle cleanse kit to clean the face, and pack it in a paddle cover to prevent scuffs. "I wipe down my paddle face once a week with water to prevent any accumulation of dirt," says Schmits.

"Keep your paddle stored in a cool, dry environment and never leave it in a hot car. Also, don't smash it when you're angry," says Johns.

Like any sport, pickleball does pose some injury risks (some games can last over 2 hours at a time). The most common injuries include tennis and golf elbow, which can be caused by swinging a paddle that's too light or too heavy—or simply by swinging it too much and not allowing for proper rest.

"Grip size, paddle weight, and swing weight (how the weight is distributed) all contribute to the efficiency and comfort of the human-paddle interface," says Schmits. "A grip that is too small may require an over-clenched grip to prevent spinning in the hand, a paddle that is too light may not have enough mass to prevent twisting on off-center shots and will transmit unwanted vibration, an overly head-heavy paddle may require more torque to snap through. Also, a paddle that is too heavy will quickly fatigue muscles, as well as slow down hand speed."

A paddle with good vibration absorption is also important, which is why a wooden paddle is a no-go if you're an active player. "Anything that absorbs more energy in the paddle and reduces the amount of vibration that travels up your arm is good at preventing soreness," says Crowley Sr.

Jeff Turbett is a fitness and wellness writer who's based in Miami, FL. His work has been featured in The Manual and FightCamp.

Ryan Brower is the Senior Gear and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he tests the best products in outdoor gear, tech, running shoes, and more. He has written about the outdoors for nearly two decades and was previously the Managing Editor, Content Performance at Gear Patrol. He holds a B.A. in Sport Management and is a Certified Beer Server, having previously covered the craft beer industry. Ryan currently lives on the water in New Jersey with his wife and their dog.

#4652. Tesla launches Robotaxi in San Antonio with a 274 sq mi geofence on paper

Tesla is launching its Robotaxi service in San Antonio, its eighth city, with a launch geofence covering about 274 square miles. That’s the biggest day-one map Tesla has ever posted, and more than four times the size of Waymo’s San Antonio service area.

But if Tesla’s recent maps are any guide, a big chunk of that area won’t be bookable. In Austin, an independent check found the Robotaxi app only accepted pickups and drop-offs in about 59% of the zone Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account made the announcement just after midnight local time: “Robotaxi available in San Antonio starting tomorrow, 5am.” It came with a map of the “launch geofence,” a large polygon that runs from Loop 1604 on the north side down to just south of downtown.

Robotaxi Tracker, which measures operator maps and logs fleet sightings, puts the zone at 274 square miles. That covers about 1.0 million residents (51% of the metro) and 721,000 jobs. San Antonio International Airport sits inside the polygon, but it isn’t served.

Waymo started driverless rides in San Antonio in February with more than 60 square miles and opened to all riders in October, airport trips included. Robotaxi Tracker currently lists Waymo’s San Antonio area at 59 square miles.

What Tesla didn’t say is how many cars will cover its 274 square miles. As of Monday morning, Robotaxi Tracker hadn’t logged a single Tesla Robotaxi in San Antonio.

The launch landed the same day Tesla expanded Austin again. The tracker now measures Tesla’s Austin zone at 443 square miles, up 178 square miles since mid-September.

We’ve seen this movie. Last month, Tesla expanded its Houston geofence into the shape of a rocket, and within two days the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app refusing downtown pickups inside it.

Since then, Koby Pierce, who tracks Tesla’s service on X, has done the tedious work of checking city after city. He searched thousands of real addresses in the Robotaxi app on an emulator and mapped only the ones where Tesla allows a pickup or drop-off, then compared that with the map Tesla advertises. Here’s the share of Tesla’s advertised land area that actually works:

Austin's dropoff/pickup Geofence is ~41% smaller than advertised.Seems mostly the East side of town is inaccessible. Unsure the cause. Any ideas?Dallas is next and should be done by noon tomrrow. pic.twitter.com/WvU99sJlJh

Austin is the one that matters. It’s Tesla’s flagship market, with 453 unsupervised vehicles in service according to Robotaxi Tracker. Yet about 41% of the advertised map Pierce tested, mostly on the east side of town, wouldn’t take a ride request. Pierce points to railroad crossings as a big factor in several cities, which lines up with the strange downtown routing we saw in Houston.

To be fair, Pierce says Waymo is next on his list, and he expects “they’re no better.” Robotaxi Tracker already had to trim Waymo’s Orlando area last month after finding the airport, inside Waymo’s published map, wasn’t selectable. We’ll look at those numbers when they’re out. But it doesn’t change what Tesla is doing with San Antonio today.

Credit where it’s due. A 274-square-mile launch in a new city is progress, and Tesla now runs unsupervised rides in eight cities. At the start of this year, it had no unsupervised rides anywhere.

But we need to stop taking Tesla’s geofence numbers at face value, and that includes us. We used Tesla’s 254-square-mile figure for Houston, and it turned out to be overstated. In all six cities Pierce has checked, the real service area is between 59% and 78% of what Tesla posts. In Austin and Miami, it’s about 60%.

So the honest way to read the San Antonio announcement is “up to 274 square miles.” In practice, expect something closer to 160 to 210 square miles, with an unknown number of cars, and the airport already off the table. That’s still bigger than Waymo’s 59 square miles in the city.

These maps are mostly fiction. I live inside the Houston map but the app says I am outside. If you drive to where the app allows, no vehicles are ever available. Waymos are a routine site and are available on a short notice. This is smoke and mirrors to shore up the company value ahead of the SpaceX merger.

The problem is that square miles are the metric Tesla fully controls. Drawing a polygon costs nothing, and the numbers were all over X within hours of the post. Cars per square mile, wait times, and rides completed are much harder to inflate, and nationally Waymo still runs over 4,000 driverless vehicles to Tesla’s 666, per Robotaxi Tracker.

I still consider this a small pilot by any standard, and safety remains the bottleneck. Tesla is still forcing riders through hour-long rides that should take 15 minutes because they have to take routes that avoid areas that Tesla can’t safely navigate without supervision.

Until that’s fixed, robotaxi won’t be able to meaningfully scale beyond these limited demonstrations in geo-fenced areas.

Robotaxi or not, most EV charging still happens at home, and pairing it with rooftop solar can cut your cost per mile to nearly zero. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4651. The Best Electrolyte Powders, Tested by Registered Dietitians

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Our team recommends formulas from Thorne, Transparent Labs, and LMNT.

ELECTROLYTE POWDERS HAVE become very trendy over the last few years, but the variety of ingredients and numerous products on the market may leave you wondering what you actually need. These powders have various amounts of sodium and other electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium, etc.), plus sugars and additional ingredients meant to improve your hydration after a sweaty workout. Based on our extensive testing, we found that these formulas are an easy and convenient way to replenish electrolytes lost in sweat. That's because sweat contains water and electrolytes, with sodium losses being the highest, says Leah Reitmayer, MS, RD, a Board-Certified Sports Dietitian and owner of Lettuce Eat Dessert.

The American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) recommends a sodium intake of 300 to 600 milligrams per hour for endurance athletes who exercise for over two hours or are considered “heavy sweaters,” losing more than 1.2 liters per hour. Important: The average person doesn’t need an electrolyte supplement after your average one-hour workout. But when you need that extra boost of hydration and electrolyte replenishment, we have the seven best electrolyte powders to choose from, according to sports dietitians and athletes.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to find the latest and greatest equipment and supplements, including electrolyte powders. I personally tested each of these products in a variety of scenarios, including as part of a morning routine, in the afternoon after work, and after intense workouts, in the gym and on the track.

I also consulted Marty Munson, Health Director at Men’s Health, triathlete, and USA Triathlon Certified Coach; and Deputy Editor Paul Kita to get their insights on the electrolyte products they have tested throughout their years in the industry. Read on for our guide to the best electrolyte powders.

*Additional reporting by Kelsey Kunik, RDN.

I’m a big fan of Thorne because they design their supplements so that they can be used by the most elite athletes but are also accessible to everyone else. This formula provides a balanced blend of sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium. And in keeping with their no-BS approach, there aren’t any sweeteners, colors, or fillers, keeping the blend non-GMO and gluten-free.

Poured into the glass, the powder dissolves quickly and completely, leaving only the color and refreshing taste. I’m a fan of the flavors, which they kept to three heavy-hitters, and if you’re not picky, I recommend the variety pack so you can switch between them.

We’ve seen that brands have been smartly moving away from carbohydrate formulas, so that you can customize your carb intake if you’re an athlete. That is the case here, with only a single gram of carbs. So if you’re looking for a quality, easy-to-drink electrolyte powder that can also travel with you, this is the best.

Transparent Labs Hydrate electrolyte powder includes multiple electrolytes and other nutrients like taurine and Senactiv, an adaptogen complex that supports muscle recovery. “It has 500 mg of sodium per serving, which fits ACSM’s recommendation for sodium replacement per hour,” says registered dietitian Sarah Alsing, MS, RD. You’ll also replace small amounts of potassium, magnesium, and calcium.

Each dose has 1,000 milligrams of taurine, a sulfur-containing amino acid that may help support muscle recovery. You can choose from six flavors, all sweetened with stevia, as this formula is carbohydrate and calorie-free.

“I look for supplements to be third-party tested so you can trust the ingredients listed, and Transparent Labs is third-party tested,” says Alsing. It’s Informed Sport Certified, meaning it’s been tested for substances banned by major athletic regulating organizations, which gives peace of mind to competing athletes.

This electrolyte powder only comes in a multi-serving tub, which could be seen as a downside if you want to take your electrolytes on the road often. But for us, it is a great way to reduce waste and if you’re taking electrolytes as part of your daily routine, you’re probably usually taking them at home.

Experts and testers we consulted with say LMNT is a serious electrolyte supplement, providing 1,000 milligrams of sodium in each pack. With this much salt, you can expect the flavor to be, well, salty. After a 10-mile run or a hard, sweaty bike ride, we appreciate the replenishment, but the salty flavor may take a little getting used to for some people. However, other athletes like Munson actually prefer that taste over some typical sports drinks, which can taste overly sweet. Personally, I tend to agree. The instructions include mixing a packet with 16 to 32 ounces of water, but you can always dilute it a little more to cut the salty flavor. I drink mine with about 12 ounces of water, and find the salty taste to be a bit stronger but still enjoyable at these proportions.

“There are several flavors to choose from, which helps finding one you will enjoy and tolerate during your workouts,” says Alsing. You can choose from fruit flavors like citrus or watermelon or even a more decadent chocolate caramel. It’s sweetened with stevia leaf, and one packet has just 2 grams of carbohydrates. If you don’t like the taste of stevia, you can always choose the raw, unflavored option with no sweeteners added. Personally, I stick to the fruity flavors as I feel the salty taste is best when combined with citrus, berry, or melon notes.

In addition to sodium, LMNT provides 200 milligrams of potassium and 60 milligrams of magnesium, electrolytes that are also lost through sweat, although in lower amounts than sodium. Personally, I find that drinking these electrolytes right in the morning keeps me better hydrated throughout the day.

Not only is Nuun Sport Powder certified gluten-free, but this product is also vegan and kosher. The Nuun tablets are effervescent, which can be difficult to drink while running or biking. But the Sport Electrolyte Tablets have no fizz, making it a better option for athletes drinking them on the go. The powder sticks come in five flavors and have just one gram of added sugars along with stevia for a sweet flavor. While many people love the packet flavors, they are a lot stronger than the tablets, which may be off-putting for some athletes if you’re drinking them during a workout.

Each packet has 300 milligrams of sodium, along with potassium and magnesium, making it a good all-around hydration drink for workouts lasting an hour or less. The packets are easy to tear and mix quickly into a water bottle for hydration on the go—no waiting for tablets to dissolve. And while Nuun is known more for their tablets, we find the powder packets to be the superior form when it comes to mid-workout hydration.

This formula has 330 milligrams of sodium in each serving and is free from gluten, soy, and certified vegan. This formula does have 7 grams of added sugars and a total of 9 grams of carbohydrates but is also one of the few that does not use stevia as a sweetener. Though 7 grams of sugar is higher than zero-sugar brands, it’s a lot less than some competitors use (for example, Liquid I.V. has 11 grams of added sugar per serving).

And unlike the other powders, this one has 15 percent DV of zinc, an essential trace mineral that helps with the absorption of water and electrolytes by the intestines, aiding hydration.If you’re looking for a zero sugar option, they have the Zero Sugar Variety which also has the addition of several B vitamins.

Liquid I.V. has been in the electrolyte game a while, but their original product contains 11 grams of added sugar. To keep up with competitors boasting formulas sans sugar, they released a sugar-free line and it does not disappoint. This updated formula is one of our favorite sugar-free electrolyte powders on the market, sweetened instead with stevia and allulose (a naturally occurring, low-calorie sugar that doesn’t spike blood glucose).

Each stick delivers 500 milligrams of sodium, which meets ACSM’s recommendations and is ideal for heavy sweaters or endurance athletes. You’ll also get 370 milligrams of potassium, but you won’t find any magnesium or calcium in this product—which could be a miss for those looking for a complete electrolyte supplement rather than the heavily sodium-focused product here.

It’s worth noting that Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free does contain vitamin C, niacin, and B vitamins, added micronutrients that many electrolyte supplements do not offer. This formula mixes easily into water and comes in unique flavors like white peach and rainbow sherbet. Just be aware that the sweetening agent allulose, while generally well-tolerated, may cause mild bloating or gas in some people.

First and foremost, not everyone needs an electrolyte powder (or an electrolyte drink) every day. In fact, the average American is getting way too much sodium in their diet, contributing to chronic health conditions like heart disease and high blood pressure. “The average man working out for an hour a day can meet their electrolyte needs through what they eat and should prioritize drinking plenty of water,” says Alsing. She recommends eating potassium-rich foods like bananas, avocados, and potatoes, and salty foods like salted nuts or pickles after a sweaty workout.

If you’re unsure whether you would benefit from an electrolyte powder, talk with a registered dietitian, or try a product like the Nix Hydration Biosensor, which measures your sweat output in real time. Marty Munson—Health Director at Men’s Health, triathlete, and USA Triathlon Certified Coach—says sweat testing played a big role in helping her customize a rehydration plan. For those who have done the research, talked to their doctors, and are sweating more than most recreational athletes, we’ve got the scoop (pun intended) on what to look for in the best electrolyte supplements below.

“You want to look for a product that contains at least 230-690mg of sodium,” says Reitmayer. This is in line with the ACSM recommendations to replace sodium losses after two hours of exercise or exercise that results in heavy sweating. Losing just 1 to 2 percent of your body weight through sweat can lead to an increased heart rate, higher core temperature, as well as decreased cardiac output, time to exhaustion, and power. Sodium helps maintain fluid retention in the body, leading to less water loss and improved hydration status as you drink water to replace what you lost through sweat.

Electrolyte powders vary widely in sugar content. We recommend looking for options with no more than 5 to 10 grams of added sugar unless you’re using it as both a hydration and carbohydrate source during longer workouts. For casual training or daily hydration, sugar-free options using stevia, monk fruit, or allulose are usually preferred. Be mindful of sugar alcohols, which can cause bloating or GI discomfort in some people.

If you want to combine your carbohydrate refueling and electrolytes in one drink, look for a formula that has a carbohydrate source. Munson explains that the trend is going away from these types of drinks, as many athletes like to have more control over their refueling source, choosing a separate powder for electrolytes and using other mixes, gels, or chews as an energy source. Some electrolyte powders have no carbohydrates, while others may contain 15 grams or more. “If you are looking for a sports drink with electrolytes, aim for 5-10% of the solution carbohydrates,” says Reitmayer.

Sodium isn’t the only electrolyte lost through sweat, even though it is the most abundant. You may also want an electrolyte powder that replaces electrolytes like potassium, magnesium, chloride, and/or zinc. While it’s helpful to replace these electrolytes as well, some athletes prefer less magnesium, as forms of this mineral can have a slight laxative effect, which you would probably want to avoid while competing.

How you plan to use your electrolyte powder should factor into the packaging you choose. Single-serving sticks or packets are great for travel, races, or throwing in your gym bag. They’re lightweight, easy to portion, and reduce mess when you’re on the move. Multi-serving tubs can be more cost-effective and environmentally friendly, but they require measuring and aren’t as convenient mid-workout or on the trail. Either way, look for resealable, moisture-resistant packaging to keep the powder fresh and free from clumping.

Electrolyte powders can be used before, during, and after exercise to help replace fluids lost during periods of long exercise or heavy sweating.

Replacing water and sodium helps to avoid the effects of dehydration, which could include an increase in heart rate, core temperature, and muscle glycogen use and a decrease in cardiac output, cognitive awareness, anaerobic power, and time to exhaustion. All of these can have negative effects on performance.

Any exercise where you’re sweating can lead to electrolyte losses. Short sweat sessions can usually be replaced with the sodium included in regular foods and drinks, while sessions longer than two hours may need a stronger source of sodium, like an electrolyte rehydration drink.

Depending on the ingredients, some electrolyte powders could lead to digestive upset, especially if they include high amounts of sugar, sugar alcohol, or magnesium. Drinking electrolyte powders when you’re not losing sodium through sweat or if you have high blood pressure could increase your blood pressure.

#4650. 4 Types of Dead-End Relationships

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

Sara and Keith have been married for nine years and have three children. Both work full-time, do their share of chores and parenting, and fill weekends and many evenings with soccer games, ballet lessons, or overflow work. Is it an okay life? Yes, they would agree it is okay, but in the next breath, they'll admit there’s little affection or intimacy between them.

I’ve met hundreds of couples like Sara and Keith whose relationship has been pushed to the back burner, and intimacy has essentially reached a dead end.

Here are four of the most common relationship patterns:

Child- or work-centered. This is Sara and Keith. Essentially, they stopped being a couple and instead became mom and pop or worker bees. Such couples often complain that they wish they had more time for couple time, but they're so busy with work and kids.

Roommates. If they don’t have the demands or distractions of work or children, many couples downshift to roommate status. They do spend time together, which they usually enjoy; they may even describe the other as their best friend, but the affection has long since dried up. And like roommates, there’s plenty of talk about schedules and chores.

Parallel lives. This takes the roommate scenario to another level. No best-friend status; no doing things together; each does their own thing; they essentially just share the same space.

Habit/routine-driven lifestyle. This can bleed into all the above variations, where, like Sara and Keith, they do what they do because they do it. They run on autopilot most of the time, and habits and routines kill any hope of spontaneity or anything different.

What holds all these types of couples together is that they're defined by bad solutions to other problems lying beneath. Here are some of the common sources:

Problems that are swept under the rug. If problems go unresolved, they stack up and act like a wedge pushing you apart. You create a long list of "things we don't talk about" and fill in the space with the demands and distractions of work and kids—or you devolve into parallel lives.

A power struggle. Here, problems are never solved because the individuals are unwilling to reach win-win compromises. Sometimes this attitude is fueled by anger and resentment from old wounds; sometimes it is simply a matter of personality—perhaps high anxiety they try to manage through control, self-centeredness, or a need for power. Neither is willing to bend because it feels like letting the other guy win, and coming out on top is always the priority.

Conflict avoidance. Some individuals have learned to fear conflict and others' strong emotions, often because of a childhood environment in which parents were frightening or modeled passivity and avoidance. As a result, anger is internalized or turned into self-blame, and problems are never discussed or resolved. Periodically, one person may act out or explode in anger, which only further fuels their fear and internalization.

Unhealed wounds. Past affairs and sudden, traumatic decisions, such as abruptly quitting jobs or being forced to move—painful incidents that shattered safety and trust and linger, coloring the relationship—have become a grudge that is always there; an open wound that never heals.

An expired relationship contract. Whatever Sara and Keith needed from each other nine years ago, they likely no longer need it now. Each has grown into different needs and desires, but like many couples, they’ve built a life in a box of rules and routines that no longer fit them. Some couples divorce; others, like them, downshift their relationship.

If you’re ready for a change—to get your relationship back on the front burner and bring back intimacy and affection—here are some tips to get you started:

Acknowledge the state of the relationship. In some ways, this can be the hardest step. Like "The Emperor's New Clothes," it requires breaking the code of silence, refusing to ignore reality, and having the courage to be honest. Once you say how you’ve been feeling and start that conversation, you can’t unsay it or the other can’t unhear it. You’ve opened the door to change, and that’s a good place to start.

Change the emotional climate through action. Resist the urge to think change is about getting the other person to change: this leads to nagging, manipulation, or a blink contest where each waits for the other. Instead, think about changing the overall emotional climate of the relationship, breaking ingrained habits and patterns, and stopping autopilot behaviors. The key is action: Plan a date night; snuggle together on the couch while you watch a movie; move the kid’s bedtime earlier so you have time as a couple to simply chat at the end of the day. Something, anything that is different and positive.

Repair old wounds. I’ve heard partners say they just need answers to questions that have been lingering for years—about the affair, the job, or the move. Or sometimes it is just the opportunity to get things off their chests and finally feel heard and understood, without avoidance or defensiveness. Sometimes you can do this on your own; sometimes it helps to start by writing a letter or email; sometimes you need to bring in a professional to help mediate and moderate the conversation.

Tackle unresolved problems. The best way to do this is to chip away at them in baby steps. I suggest that couples set aside a good time to talk when they’re not tired or distracted. Treat it like a staff meeting at work: Set an agenda with one or two items, focus on you, and work toward a win-win compromise while controlling your emotions. Meet for 30-45 minutes. And if it is hard to do, bring in a professional.

Resist the urge to think your feelings need to change before you can act; if you keep doing what you’re doing, you’ll keep feeling the same way. Instead, challenge yourself to break out and take action.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

Taibbi, R. (2019). Doing couple therapy. New York: Guilford.

#4649. LiveWire just showed off its biggest electric motorcycle lineup yet

LiveWire has spent the last few years expanding beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off. But seeing the company’s latest machines all together at EICMA in Milan really drives home just how much broader LiveWire’s ambitions have become.

I stopped by the LiveWire booth at EICMA 2026, where the company had everything from its new lightweight S4 Honcho models to the freshly acquired DUST electric dirt bikes – plus STACYC’s electric balance bikes for the youngest riders.

It’s quite a spread, and perhaps more importantly, it paints a picture of a company that increasingly wants to have an electric two-wheeler for just about every stage of a rider’s life.

I also had a chance to spend several hours test-riding the S4 Honcho Street in Milan, so be on the lookout for that article and video to experience it with me.

But for now, let’s see what was at the LiveWire booth.

Perhaps the most important bikes at the booth were the S4 Honcho models, LiveWire’s new lightweight and lower-cost electric motorcycles.

The production S4 Honcho Street made its European debut at EICMA alongside the dirt-oriented S4 Honcho Trail. The Trail version recently began reaching customers in the US, with the Street now en route to dealerships, and European sales are beginning around the EICMA launch.

These bikes represent a significant departure from LiveWire’s earlier strategy. Instead of trying to compete directly with full-size gasoline motorcycles on outright performance, the Honcho platform is aimed at riders looking for something smaller, simpler, and more approachable.

And now the family is getting even bigger.

Also on display was the new S4 Honcho Skate, making its first public appearance.

The Skate is planned for 2027 and further expands the modular Honcho platform with a stripped-down, playful design.

For those who have followed H-D’s electric ambitions for as long as I have, you might even remember the original Harley-Davidson electric moped prototype that seems to have served as inspiration for the Honcho Skate’s design.

Seeing the various Honcho versions together also makes LiveWire’s strategy with the platform much clearer. Rather than creating one small electric motorcycle, the company is building an entire family around the concept.

The other major attraction at LiveWire’s booth was the DUST lineup.

LiveWire acquired the assets of DUST Moto earlier this year, bringing the lightweight electric dirt bike company under its umbrella. EICMA marked the first public showing of the production-intent DUST Hightail under LiveWire ownership.

The Hightail had already generated plenty of interest before the acquisition as a lightweight, high-performance electric dirt bike. Now we’re getting our first look at how that machine fits into LiveWire’s broader plans.

The company is targeting a 2027 introduction for the production Hightail.

LiveWire also showed the new DUST Spur, another model planned for 2027 and intended to expand the newly formed DUST family.

The DUST acquisition is particularly interesting because it gives LiveWire an immediate foothold in the rapidly growing lightweight electric off-road motorcycle space without having to develop an entirely new platform from scratch.

In what could be a hint at faster charging to come, there was an interesting S2 Alpanista Corsa motorcycle that had been outfitted with a NACS plug and DC fast-charging capabilities.

LiveWire claimed a 20-80% charge in under 10 minutes, which would revolutionize the ability to do long-distance motorcycle touring, or just make it more convenient to get a quick charge and head back to your apartment.

There’s on word on whether the concept will make it to production, but the specs are enticing!

The most interesting part of LiveWire’s EICMA display may not have been any individual motorcycle, but rather what happens when you stand back and look at the entire booth.

On one end you’ve got STACYC electric balance bikes. LiveWire says the brand has already introduced more than 250,000 riders to two wheels.

Then you’ve got the lightweight S4 Honcho family. Above that sit the DUST machines for more serious off-road riding, while LiveWire’s existing S2 motorcycles continue to cover the higher-performance street end of the spectrum.

That’s becoming something of an electric two-wheeler ladder.

A kid can theoretically start on a STACYC, graduate into increasingly capable electric two-wheelers, and eventually wind up on a proper electric motorcycle – all within the same corporate family.

And that feels particularly relevant at a show like EICMA, where much of the motorcycle industry is still trying to figure out exactly where electric motorcycles fit.

LiveWire seems increasingly convinced that the answer isn’t simply to build electric replacements for existing gasoline motorcycles.

Instead, the company is spreading out into categories where electric drivetrains can create different kinds of motorcycles altogether.

I’ve been following LiveWire’s evolution for years, and the company standing in front of me at EICMA looks considerably different from the one that started out selling a single expensive flagship electric motorcycle.

The big, high-performance bikes are still important, but machines like the S4 Honcho and DUST Hightail are arguably more interesting to me because they can bring entirely different riders into electric motorcycling.

They’re smaller. They’re simpler. And perhaps most importantly, they’re targeting the kind of fun, accessible riding that doesn’t require superbike levels of performance.

There’s still plenty we need to learn about several of these new models, particularly final specifications and pricing for the 2027 machines.

But seeing the Honcho, Honcho Skate, Hightail, Spur, and STACYC machines together at EICMA makes one thing pretty clear: LiveWire isn’t just trying to sell a few electric motorcycles anymore.

It’s trying to build an entire electric two-wheeler ecosystem.

#4648. How You Can Use an Upper-Lower Workout Split for More Gains

If you want to build strength and muscle, split your workout plan in two.

THE STRUCTURE OF your workout over the course of weeks and months should depend on more than just the latest fitness fad. When you’re working toward a goal—whether that’s tied to building muscle, forging strength, losing weight, or improving performance—you’ll have the most success if you follow a plan. That plan (often called a workout split) should take into account arange of factors, including your specific goals, your experience level, schedule, and available equipment.

And one of the most well-known (and easy-to-understand) approaches to this is the Upper-Lower split, which is one of several workout splits organized around training different parts of the body on different days.

An Upper-Lower Split program is broken down exactly as its name implies. One day you’ll train the muscle groups in your upper body (think chest, shoulders, back, arms); then the next you’ll train your lower body muscles (quads, glutes, hamstrings, calves). In general, that means your upper body gets to recover on days you’re training your lower body, and vice versa.

This approach is one of a handful of training splits that works very well if you’re trying to add muscle, or if you’re somebody who’s chasing body recomposition. If you’re trying to build muscle, the more frequently you can train a muscle group with effective, hard sets, the better.

And an upper-lower split lets you train each muscle group at least twice a week, with solid rest in between each session. You’re training each muscle group more frequently than you would if you were doing a bro split (training just one body part a day). And you’re able to do more sets and exercises for key muscle groups than you would if you were doing a full-body training split.

Let’s break down the details of the upper-lower of split, along with a sample session you can use to put it into practice.

Sets and reps: 3 sets of 8 to 10 steps per leg

Sets and reps: 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps per leg

IF YOU WANT to understand the logic behind the workout above, here’s what you need to know. You'll alternate focusing on the upper body muscles and the lower body muscles in this split. Since you're no longer training the entire body, you'll have the time and energy to include a few more accessory motions. Over the course of the week, aim to hit all of the following movement patterns.

There are multiple ways to build an upper-lower split depending on your goals. But in general, think about including three to five exercises in every session.

YOU’RE ABLE TO hit major muscle groups more completely by splitting the body in half. Since we're able to add in a few accessory motions, we can start training in several different planes of motion, too. This split is well suited for recovery, since your upper body rests while you're working the lower body, and vice versa. That allows you to increase your frequency of training.

YOU’RE STILL WORKING quite a few major muscle groups in a single workout, which can be fatiguing for the accessory movements added onto the end. If you’re in the awkward schedule space between having three and four days you can train, you might struggle to hit the upper/lower/upper/lower cadence that will be most effective—so stick to the more flexible full-body split.

#4647. BYD is going all out on its ultra-luxury EV with coach doors and 1,000+ km of range [Images]

BYD unveiled the Yangwang Altior, its new ultra-luxury EV with coach doors, over 1,000 km of CTLC range, a 1,000V fast-charging platform, and plenty of premium extras.

The “super-luxury executive flagship sedan,” as BYD calls it, made its official debut in Abu Dhabi, UAE, over the weekend.

For those who don’t know, Yangwang is BYD’s ultra-luxury sub-brand, sitting at the very top of its brand hierarchy.

The Atrio is Yangwang’s largest and most luxurious sedan, set to compete with high-end brands like Rolls-Royce, Bentley, and Mercedes-Benz Maybach.

Measuring 5,600 mm long, 2,030 mm wide, and 1,590 mm tall, with a 3,500 mm wheelbase, BYD’s flagship sedan sits squarely between the Rolls-Royce Ghost and Phantom (standard wheelbase) in length.

BYD said the “Golden Body Proportions” are designed to maximize interior space for both front and rear passengers.

Its meticulous front-end design is inspired by “Ding,” a traditional ancient Chinese cauldron, featuring “diamond-cut” headlights, a 137-gemstone dot-matrix grille, and, to top it off, a 24K pure gold car emblem sits up front and center.

The coach doors create a grand entrance, with the front doors opening at an 80-degree angle and the rear doors opening to a 90-degree angle.

Inside, the flagship sedan takes luxury up a notch with a massive, full-length panoramic center infotainment screen that extends from the driver to the passenger side.

The “Wrap-around cockpit” is designed to create an immersive, premium experience, with four executive seats and a central island for rear passengers that includes vehicle controls, storage, and even a champagne glass holder.

BYD said it offers the most second-row space in its class, but didn’t reveal specifics. The zero-gravity “cloud-like” rear seats feature a four-ball mechanical massage head, you know, for those longer trips.

Meanwhile, the front passenger seat can fold at the push of a button to open up more space for rear passengers.

The interior features premium materials, including full-grain genuine leather seats, diamond-cut detailing, real wood trim, and natural lambswool foot pads.

And that’s not all. It also has a 39-speaker Dynaudio Platinum Evidence high-end sound system that creates an immersive 360-degree “hall-level” sound experience.

The Yangwang Altio is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough tech, including a high-speed tire-blowout stability system, emergency float mode, and in-place U-turn or tank-turn control using its quad-motor e4 platform.

It's main rival is the Maextro S800, which wasn't in the list.

It also uses BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Fast Charging Technology, which provides a CLTC driving range of over 1,000 km (621 miles).

The flagship sedan features “extremely fast flash charging,” BYD said, thanks to its 1000V ultra flash charging tech. It takes just five minutes to charge the vehicle’s battery from 10% to 70%. To go from 10% to 97% it takes just nine minutes.

BYD opened orders for the limited-edition “Mountain and River Rhyme” Yangwang Altrio model, which will be extremely exclusive with just 399 units.

Buyers can place a reservation with a 300,000 yuan ($45,000) deposit. BYD didn’t reveal final prices, but the global version is expected to start at around 2 million yuan ($300,000).

#4646. Musk admits Tesla doesn’t have enough talent to build more than one car at a time after exodus

Elon Musk now says Tesla can’t build the Cybertruck and the Cybercab at the same time because there are only so many “smart, dedicated people” to go around. Half the executives he showed off in 2023 as proof of Tesla’s “bench strength” have since left the company.

It’s the most honest explanation yet for how Tesla went from five consumer vehicle programs at the start of 2026 to a single platform, Model 3 and Model Y, by the middle of 2027.

On Friday, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around the middle of next year “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” As we pointed out at the time, Giga Texas isn’t short on space. The Cybertruck line runs at a fraction of its installed capacity because the truck sells a fraction of what Tesla planned.

A day later, replying to a user on X, Musk gave a different reason:

“The biggest thing most people fail to understand is that there are a very limited number of smart, dedicated people! They can only do so many things.”

He added that if Tesla has to “maintain a complex production line, supply chain and allocate engineering for Cybertruck, we can’t use those people” for scaling Cybercab.

By this morning, the explanation had shifted again, to the “opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck.” But the Saturday version is the one that matters. Musk is telling us the bottleneck at Tesla isn’t factory space or money. It’s people.

The Cybertruck is the second casualty this year. In January, Musk announced the end of the Model S and Model X on Tesla’s Q4 earnings call and summed up the reason in one word: “Autonomy.” The Fremont line is being converted to build Optimus robots, and by April, only inventory was left.

The flagships had been on life support for years. Their last real update was the 2021 interior refresh. The June 2025 “refresh” brought a new paint color, a front bumper camera, a bit more range, and a $5,000 price increase. That’s not how you treat a vehicle program you care about.

Tesla painted a very different picture just two years ago. At its 2024 shareholder meeting, it showed this slide of its lineup: the Model 3, Model Y, Model S, Model X, Cybertruck, and Semi, plus three vehicles under covers that Musk said were “going to be pretty special.”

Of the five consumer vehicles on that slide, three are now dead or on their way out.

So here’s what will be left in the second half of 2027: Model 3 and Model Y, two vehicles built on the same platform, plus the Model Y L and cheaper “Standard” variants of both. The Semi is a commercial truck. The Roadster’s production is still a giant question mark. And the Cybercab is a robotaxi with no steering wheel, not a car you can buy – even though Tesla is going to let fleet buyers get them to add on its own Robotaxi network. We previously explained how this is a terrible idea.

For comparison, Hyundai Motor Group sells more than half a dozen EV models in the US across its Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis brands, on top of its gas and hybrid lineup. GM and Toyota run dozens of nameplates at once. Tesla can’t keep more than two programs alive at the same time.

At Tesla’s Investor Day at Giga Texas on March 1, 2023, Musk mostly stayed out of the spotlight. Instead, Tesla paraded more than a dozen executives on stage to present its plans, a rare move for a company long criticized for being a one-man show.

“We’ve obviously got significant bench strength here,” Musk said at the time.

Of the 14 executives named as presenters that day, seven are gone:

Martin Viecha, who ran investor relations through that event, left in April 2024 as well.

Seven are still at Tesla, according to their LinkedIn profiles: Tom Zhu, Lars Moravy, Franz von Holzhausen, Ashok Elluswamy, Karn Budhiraj, Laurie Shelby, and Brandon Ehrhart. And the ones who left weren’t peripheral. They ran batteries, powertrain, software, chips, energy, charging, and the money.

The bigger problem for Tesla’s ability to run vehicle programs is the program-level talent, the people who take a car from prototype to volume production.

In November 2025, Tesla lost the head of its Cybertruck program, Siddhant Awasthi, and the Model Y program manager, Emmanuel Lamacchia, within a day of each other. Lamacchia had led Tesla’s best-selling vehicle for four years.

Then the Cybercab, the program Musk is now pulling people toward, started losing its own leaders:

Add 17-year finance VP Sendil Palani and Thomas Dmytryk, the director who built Tesla’s over-the-air update system and Robotaxi infrastructure, both in March, and you get the picture.

So when Musk says he needs Cybertruck’s people for Cybercab, part of the reason is that Cybercab keeps losing its own.

Musk will frame all of this as focus. Autonomy is going to be so big, the argument goes, that Tesla has to go all in.

But we’ve heard that before. Tesla made the yoke steering wheel standard on the Model S and Model X in 2021 because the cars would soon drive themselves, then brought back a round wheel as an option. It removed the turn signal stalk from the Model 3 in 2023, then brought the stalk back in 2025 and started selling a $350 retrofit to owners. Each time, the autonomy that justified the change wasn’t there yet.

And Tesla isn’t the leader in unsupervised driving. It has the best driver-assist system on the market, but Waymo still logs roughly seven times more driverless miles per week, and NHTSA estimates Tesla’s entire Robotaxi fleet at about 1,000 vehicles. Zoox is scaling too, and Baidu’s Apollo Go runs a far bigger driverless fleet in China.

This is something that I’ve been highlighting for a decade. Even after it became a big company with a large headcount, Tesla has never been good at running several vehicle programs in a healthy way. The Model S and Model X were starved for updates long before the talent exodus started. Tesla has always thrown everything at its newest program and let the older ones coast.

What changed is that the slack is gone. In 2023, Tesla could still neglect the flagships and keep them on the market, because it had deep benches in engineering, manufacturing, and software to absorb mistakes. Today, half the executives Musk called his bench are gone, and the people running the Cybercab ramp keep walking out. Musk is now openly telling us there aren’t enough people left to build a pickup truck and a robotaxi at the same time.

Musk calls it focus. It looks a lot more like a constraint Tesla can’t hire its way out of.

Tesla never had the capacity to hire, organize, manage and retain the amount of human talent required to develop multiple car model lines in concert. Tesla barely paid its staff enough for one model line development.

You only need to look at other companies with decades of experience in developing many, separate (but technically strongly overlapping) model lines to see how much does that require in terms of human resources and in terms of R&D cost. Like BMW has always been investing ~5 billion EUR every year in R&D. That is how you have ~14 core models with at least another dozen specialist models and more regional models plus Mini and RR on top. At times up to 60 different significant variants with different drivetrains also impacting design, logistics and production. All being always in development for the next generation and also for a mid-life refresh or two. Across the whole group, including maintenance work, there can easily be triple-digit number of vehicle model projects going at the same time.

Will the Cybercab be revolutionary and make it all worth it? We have our doubts. Tesla leads in driver assistance with FSD, but it has failed to evolve the product into unsupervised self-driving at scale, which it promised to buyers for a decade. It’s clearly not the leader in unsupervised self-driving, and the competition is crowded. Tesla’s lasting impact on the robotaxi market is genuinely hard to predict.

What’s not hard to see is the trend. Tesla has shown a complete inability to sustain multiple vehicle programs at once, and it’s getting harder for the automaker, not easier. If Tesla can’t hold on to the people who build its cars, how long before the Model 3 and Model Y get the same treatment as the Model S?

Both vehicle programs will undoubtedly go down in history as some of the most critical EVs of all time, but that doesn’t guarantee lasting success in a rapidly changing auto landscape.

If you’re driving an EV, the people building it matter, but so does where your electricity comes from. #4645. Anorexia and the Gut-Brain Connection

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

For generations, scientists and doctors believed the brain was the unquestioned command center of the body. It sent instructions and the rest of the body obeyed. Today, we know the relationship is far more complicated.

Your digestive tract is home to an intricate network of more than 100 million nerve cells—so many, in fact, that scientists often refer to it as the body's second brain. Known as the enteric nervous system, this remarkable network coordinates digestion, communicates with the immune system, influences hormone production, and remains in constant contact with the brain inside your skull.

These two "brains" are linked by an elaborate communication system known as the gut-brain axis. Messages travel in both directions, carried by nerves, hormones, immune cells, and chemical messengers produced by the trillions of bacteria that live within the intestines. It's a constant conversation—one that helps regulate not only digestion, but also mood, stress, appetite, memory, and behavior.

This discovery has transformed the way we think about both physical and mental health.

For decades, psychiatrists understandably focused almost exclusively on the brain. Depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, ADHD, and anorexia nervosa were viewed as disorders of brain chemistry. But over the past 20 years, an explosion of research has revealed that the gut is an active participant in all of these conditions. Rather than functioning as separate organs, the gut and the brain operate as partners. When one suffers, the other often does, too.

That insight is especially important in anorexia nervosa.

For people with anorexia nervosa, this two-way conversation has profound implications. Recovery isn’t only about restoring body weight or correcting abnormalities in the brain. It’s also about rebuilding a healthy digestive system capable of supporting the brain’s healing processes.

One of the cruelest aspects of anorexia nervosa is that the illness often convinces people that food and eating are problems.

As recovery begins and eating increases, many patients experience bloating, constipation, abdominal pain, nausea, and a feeling of fullness after only a few bites. These symptoms can be frightening. They seem to confirm the eating disorder's central lie: See? Eating makes you feel worse.

But that's not what's happening. In most cases, these digestive symptoms are not caused by eating. They are caused by starvation.

When the body is deprived of adequate nourishment for weeks, months, or years, it begins conserving energy wherever it can. Digestion slows dramatically. The muscles that normally move food through the stomach and intestines become less active. The stomach empties more slowly, intestinal motility decreases, and constipation becomes common. Food remains in the digestive tract longer than it should, producing bloating, abdominal discomfort, and an uncomfortable sense of fullness after meals.

Ironically, the very symptoms that make eating difficult are often the result of not eating enough in the first place.

Understanding this dynamic can be enormously reassuring as it shows that the digestive system has not been permanently damaged. The symptoms are signs of a body adapting to prolonged starvation and so, as nutritional rehabilitation progresses and the gut begins receiving the nourishment it needs, digestive function usually improves—although it often takes weeks or months for the gastrointestinal tract to recover fully.

In anorexia, another important change occurs deep within the intestines, where trillions of bacteria collectively known as the gut microbiome reside. These microorganisms help digest food, produce vitamins, regulate immune function, maintain the integrity of the intestinal lining, and manufacture compounds that influence the brain. Like every other living organism in the body, they depend on a steady supply of nutrients to thrive.

When food intake becomes severely restricted, then, the microbiome changes as well.

Over the past decade, researchers have consistently found that people with anorexia nervosa have a gut microbiome that differs significantly from those of healthy individuals. Some beneficial bacterial species decline, while others become more abundant. Overall microbial diversity—the hallmark of a healthy ecosystem—often decreases. These changes are now believed to contribute not only to digestive symptoms, but also to inflammation, anxiety, and difficulties with weight restoration.

The good news is that the gut is remarkably resilient. Unlike many organs, the digestive tract is constantly renewing itself. Cells lining the intestines are replaced every few days. The microbiome is continually adapting to changes in diet, medications, stress, and environment. Even after prolonged starvation, the digestive system has an extraordinary capacity for recovery—provided it receives the nourishment and support it needs.

Eating enough food. No supplement can substitute for dietary rehabilitation. Restoring adequate calories, protein, healthy fats, and food-delivered vitamins and minerals remains the cornerstone of recovery from anorexia nervosa.

Digestive enzymes. Digestive discomfort can make every meal feel like a battle. Bloating, cramping, constipation, and abdominal pain often reinforce the fear that eating is making things worse. Breaking that cycle sometimes requires giving the digestive system additional support while it heals. One of the simplest ways to do that is through digestive enzyme supplementation.

Digestive enzymes help break food into smaller molecules that can be more easily absorbed by the body. Although digestive enzyme supplements have not yet been studied in anorexia, decades of clinical experience suggest they can can substantially reduce gastrointestinal discomfort during nutritional rehabilitation.

Probiotics. Another important tool is the use of probiotics—live, beneficial microorganisms that help restore a healthier balance within the gut microbiome. For centuries, traditional cultures have consumed probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, kimchi, miso, and sauerkraut. Today, probiotic supplements provide carefully selected bacteria strains that can help replenish beneficial microbes disrupted by illness, antibiotics, stress, and prolonged food restrictions. Their companion nutrients, known as prebiotics, serve as food for these beneficial bacteria, helping them grow and flourish.

Learn more in my new book, Finally Nourished: A Science-Based Plan to Correct Malnutrition in Anorexia Nervosa—and Achieve True and Lasting Recovery.

Kleiman SC, et al. The Intestinal Microbiota in Acute Anorexia Nervosa and During Renourishment: Relationship to Depression, Anxiety, and Eating Disorder Psychopathology. Psychosomatic Medicine. 2015 Nov-Dec;77(9):969-81. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4643361/

Fan Y, et al. The gut microbiota contributes to the pathogenesis of anorexia nervosa in humans and mice. Nature Microbiology. 2023 May;8(5):787-802. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10159860/
